• YAML only. Easy to validate, but too weak for transformations.
  • YAML plus Python. Full power, but SQL users must wrap queries in code.
  • YAML plus SQL. Familiar for SQL users, but no escape for logic SQL cannot express.
  • YAML plus both. Covers both audiences. Needs a rule for how inputs reach the body.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
YAML plus both. YAML declares every model. The body is either a Python callable or a SQL body. The inputs map binds local aliases to ref or source.

  • A Python callable is called as build(ctx, **inputs). Each alias becomes a keyword argument holding a relation.
  • SQL refers to aliases as table names. The engine registers them as named relations for that query only.
  • At compile time pipeloom imports nothing from the project. Validation layer L6 parses the callable's file with ast to check that the function exists and that its parameters equal ctx plus the input aliases.
  • Opt-in SQL table-reference checking through the sqlglot extra warns on mismatch.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Graphs are cheap to build, so Airflow can parse DAG files safely.
  • No Jinja templating.
  • Reads of undeclared tables through ctx.engine.native are a documented escape hatch outside lineage.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0004: Plugin discovery via entry points; eight groups
docs.text: Architecture: Section 6, Plugin system and plugin API version

docs.title: Context
docs.text: pipeloom needs engines, catalogs, state stores, sinks, secret providers, executors, renderers and naming strategies to be supplied by separately installed distributions, without the core importing them.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Entry points (stdlib importlib.metadata, the pytest model). No new dependency.
  • pluggy. Built for 1:N hook fan-out.
  • A dbt-style namespace import. Couples plugin layout to import paths.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Entry points. pipeloom picks one implementation per role by kind, which is 1-of-N selection, not hook fan-out, so pluggy adds a dependency without a matching need.

  • Eight groups: pipeloom.engines, pipeloom.catalogs, pipeloom.state_stores, pipeloom.sinks, pipeloom.secret_providers, pipeloom.executors, pipeloom.renderers, pipeloom.naming.
  • Each entry point resolves to a PluginSpec(name, kind, api_version, factory, config_model, compatible_engines).
  • Discovery reads metadata only. A plugin is imported only when a config names its kind. pipeloom plugins list imports nothing.
  • PIPELOOM_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 restricts loading to --plugin module:spec.
  • A duplicate kind within a group is error PLU002.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No extra dependency, and listing plugins is safe on locked-down hosts.
  • Plugins are versioned against the plugin API version (ADR-0016).
  • No hook fan-out. If a later feature needs it, this ADR must be revisited.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended by ADR-0017: the spec gains group, capabilities and description, built-ins come from an in-code table, and PLU003 is added.

docs.title: ADR-0005: Packaging
docs.text: Architecture: Section 17, ADR-0005 text

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The core and the engine, orchestrator and lineage integrations have different dependencies and release needs. Users should install only what they run.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• One distribution with extras. Its entry points are registered even when the extra's dependencies are missing, which leads to import errors at load. It also couples dependency bounds.
  • Separate distributions in separate repositories. High overhead.
  • Separate pipeloom-<plugin> distributions in one uv workspace.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The uv workspace.

  • The core is distribution pipeloom at the repo root. Plugins live in plugins/pipeloom-<name>/ with import package pipeloom_<name> (no namespace packages).
  • Convenience extras on pipeloom (for example pipeloom[polars]) just depend on the plugin distribution.
  • PyPI now: publish pipeloom 0.0.2 only. Plugin names are published with their first functional release, which avoids PEP 541 placeholder squatting.
  • Pending trusted publishers may be registered for the plugin names. Assumption: a pending publisher does not reserve a name (unverified).
  • [tool.uv.workspace] is added in 0.2 with the first plugin. Whether uv accepts an empty members glob is unverified.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One repository and one lockfile, with separate dependency bounds per plugin.
  • Plugin names stay unclaimed on PyPI until their first functional release, so someone else could register one in the meantime.
  • Lockstep versions apply during 0.x (ADR-0016).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0006: Ready-queue scheduler
docs.text: Architecture: Section 8, Execution and scheduler

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Running a graph level by level makes every unit in a level wait for the slowest one (lesson L6). Scheduling must be deterministic so runs are reproducible and testable.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Level barriers. Simple, but idle workers wait at each level.
  • A ready queue with no level barrier. Starts a unit as soon as its parents are done.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A ready-queue scheduler with no level barrier.

  • When a unit reaches a terminal state, each child's count of pending parents goes down by one. A child whose count reaches zero is enqueued.
  • Ready units are ordered by descending count of downstream units, then by name, which is deterministic.
  • workers caps concurrency. pool tags (a later milestone) cap per-resource concurrency.
  • Policies: retries with exponential backoff and jitter (transient errors only unless retry_on: any), per-unit timeouts, cooperative cancellation with cancel_grace, skip-downstream by default with --fail-fast as an option, and a StateStore.lock concurrency guard per project and target.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Property tests (hypothesis) check the invariants: a unit starts only after all parents succeed, and every unit reaches exactly one terminal state.
  • Thread-executor timeouts are cooperative: code that ignores cancellation keeps running until the process ends. The process executor kills the child.
  • With boundary: task the orchestrator owns retries.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0007: Data handoff: execution units, inlining, intermediates
docs.text: Architecture: Section 8, ADR-0007

docs.title: Context
docs.text: With boundary: task, each unit runs in its own process or orchestrator task, so no in-memory or temporary-view handoff is possible (lesson L7).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Persisted intermediates everywhere. Simple, but costs IO.
  • Inlining everywhere. No extra IO, but recomputes shared work.
  • A hybrid, decided at compile time.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The hybrid.

  • ephemeral models are inlined. Their bodies run inside each consuming unit. Under boundary: process the result is memoized per run, so it is computed once.
  • intermediate models are persisted to <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model> (or a scratch schema the catalog provides). Finalize deletes them after intermediate_ttl.
  • view creates a catalog view where the engine supports it, never a session view.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The same plan runs in one process or many.
  • PLP406 warns when an ephemeral model fans out to more than ephemeral_fanout_warn (default 3) units and suggests intermediate.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0008: Incremental key, watermark state, strategies
docs.text: Architecture: Section 9, Incremental processing, write strategies, schema change

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Incremental logic must be declared, not inferred (lesson L12), and must survive crashes and orchestrator retries. Every write option must be applied by each strategy or rejected (L9).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Watermark kept in the target (max(column) of the target). No extra store, but needs the target to exist and read access to it.
  • Watermark in a StateStore with compare-and-swap. Works for targets that cannot be queried cheaply, at the cost of a store.
  • Both, selected per model with watermark_source: state | target.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A declared key plus a lookback, with watermarks in a StateStore. watermark_source: target reads max(column) of the target instead.

  • Per unit: determine is_incremental, read the watermark w, filter the input with filter_since(input, column, w - lookback), write, then cas_watermark(expected=w, new=max_value(filtered input)). A CAS failure is PLM203.
  • State stores: sqlite (core, local), json (core, atomic rename), table (spark plugin). boundary: task requires table or json on a shared path.
  • Strategies: append, overwrite, replace_partitions, merge, scd2. Each returns a WriteResult.
  • Idempotency: each write receives token = "<run_id>:<model>". Engines without idempotent writes declare idempotent_writes=False.
  • on_schema_change: fail (default), ignore, append_new_columns, sync_all_columns.
  • Maintenance (optimize, vacuum, clustering) runs only from maintenance: blocks, never by default.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The watermark is committed after the write. A crash between the two reprocesses at most the lookback window plus the batch. That is safe for merge, overwrite and replace_partitions, and for append only when the engine has idempotent writes (otherwise PLC505 forbids retries).
  • A schema change under the default policy fails the unit (PLM202). Every detected change emits model.schema_changed.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0009: Expectations and quarantine
docs.text: Architecture: Section 10, Data quality

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Data quality is a first-class feature (lesson L13). Rules need a clear action when a row or a dataset violates them, and failing rows should not vanish silently.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Fail-only checks. Simple, but one bad row stops the run.
  • DLT-style actions (warn, drop, fail) plus quarantine. Lets users choose per rule, and keeps dropped rows for inspection.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
DLT-style actions plus quarantine, evaluated after the transformation and before the write.

  • Row-level checks: not_null, accepted_values, range, regex, expr. Actions: warn, drop, fail.
  • Aggregate checks: unique, row_count, freshness. Actions: warn, fail. drop is PLP403.
  • EngineSession.evaluate computes every row-level predicate in one aggregate pass and returns per-expectation passed and failed counts. Unlike DLT, counts are kept on fail too.
  • drop filters rows that fail any drop predicate. If max_drop_ratio is exceeded, the unit fails with PLQ301.
  • With quality.quarantine: true, dropped rows go to <target>__quarantine with _pipeloom_run_id, _pipeloom_failed and _pipeloom_ts.
  • Lazy engines may cache the relation before the counting pass. The engine decides, and the decision is recorded in the metadata.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Results appear in run_results.json and in model.quality_evaluated events.
  • Expressions in expr checks use the engine's dialect and are not portable.
  • A quarantine table is extra storage that users must manage.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0010: Events, sinks, artifacts; rich for the console
docs.text: Architecture: Section 11, Events, logs and run metadata

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Logs, metrics, artifacts and lineage should not each have their own plumbing (lesson L1). Runs must also leave structured metadata that can be queried later.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Separate logging, metrics and lineage paths. Each is simple alone, but they drift apart.
  • One typed event stream with subscribers.
  • Console library: rich gives styled tables, colors and live progress in one dependency. structlog would still need a renderer for those. JSON lines need only the stdlib.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
One typed stream (pipeloom.event/1) and a synchronous in-process bus.

  • The envelope carries id, run_id, invocation_id, seq, ts, type, level, unit_id, model, attempt, data and context. Cross-invocation ordering is by (ts, invocation_id, seq).
  • The bus fans out to sinks in configured order. Each sink has a failure_budget (default 5 consecutive errors). When exhausted the sink is disabled and sink.disabled goes to the remaining sinks.
  • buffered: true wraps a sink in a bounded queue and worker thread, with drop-oldest and a count of drops.
  • A redaction filter masks registered secret values before any sink sees an event.
  • Built-in sinks: console, jsonl, file, artifacts (always on). pipeloom-openlineage maps units to OpenLineage jobs.
  • The console uses rich. JSON lines use the stdlib.
  • Artifacts: manifest.json (pipeloom.manifest/1) and run_results.json (pipeloom.run_results/1), with per-model and per-run metadata.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Any consumer (console, files, lineage) is a sink, and tests can assert ordered events with RecordingSink.
  • A slow sink on the synchronous bus slows the run unless it is buffered.
  • JVM traces are trimmed on the console. The full trace goes to JSON events only.
  • The OpenLineage output-statistics facet is used if available (unverified).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0011: Databricks job rendering
docs.text: Architecture: Section 12, The Databricks plugin

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A plan must run as one Databricks job, with run history, repair and the platform's own scheduling, and the same plan must also run locally.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• One task per unit as python_wheel_task, in a saved job. Gives run history, repair, only-subset runs and up to 1,000 tasks.
  • runs/submit (ephemeral). No saved job, but limited to 100 tasks and no repair history. Kept for --ephemeral dev runs.
  • Fewer, fused tasks. Needed only above the task limit (databricks.task_grouping).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each unit becomes one python_wheel_task running pipeloom run --manifest ... --select unit:<id> --expect-plan-hash <h> --run-id ....

  • Task keys are sanitized model names, truncated with a short hash suffix (assumed 100-character limit, unverified).
  • Compute: serverless by default, with one environments[] entry pinning the pipeloom distributions to the running version (environment_version is an assumed field, unverified). compute: job_cluster is the alternative.
  • The default is a saved job found by tag pipeloom_job=<project>.<pipeline>.<target>: jobs/create, or reset when it exists, then run-now. Settings: max_concurrent_runs: 1, queueing, parameters pipeloom_run_id and full_refresh.
  • pipeloom databricks bundle writes a deterministic resources/pipeloom_<project>.job.yml. pipeloom databricks deploy uses the SDK directly.
  • An empty pipeloom_run_id resolves to dbx-<job.run_id>. Each task writes its unit file to artifacts.root and publishes taskValues (capped well under 48 KiB). A final pipeloom__finalize task (run_if: ALL_DONE) writes run_results.json.
  • Above 1,000 tasks the plan fails with PLD001 and a hint to use task grouping or split by selector. No automatic job chaining before 1.0.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One job definition, whether it is triggered from the CLI, the Databricks UI or Airflow (ADR-0012).
  • Repair keeps the job run id, so the pipeloom run_id is stable and the attempt number increments.
  • pipeloom databricks run --select resolves to task keys plus finalize and uses only.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0012: Airflow rendering and modes
docs.text: Architecture: Section 13, The Airflow plugin

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Teams that orchestrate with Airflow need the pipeline graph as DAG tasks, with Airflow retries, assets and the same run identity as other orchestrators. Airflow DAG files are parsed often, so parsing must be safe and cheap.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
For the DATABRICKS mode:

  • (a) DatabricksWorkflowTaskGroup with DatabricksTaskOperator children. Builds the job spec from Airflow operators at parse time. That duplicates the pipeloom renderer, forces job name <dag_id>.<group_id>, fixes max_concurrent_runs=1, and disables "Repair All Failed Tasks" on Airflow 3.
  • (b) One run-now of the bundle-deployed job, with per-model status mirroring.

For the plugin overall: support Airflow 2 and 3, or Airflow 3 only.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Airflow 3 only (airflow.sdk, version >= 3.0). Dropping Airflow 2 support was accepted on 2026-10-29.

  • Load methods: MANIFEST (recommended) reads a precompiled manifest.json. PROJECT compiles YAML, which is safe because no user code runs (ADR-0003). Neither imports engines or connects to anything.
  • Modes: LOCAL, VIRTUALENV, KUBERNETES (wraps KubernetesPodOperator), DATABRICKS. DOCKER is later.
  • Shared behavior: one Airflow task per unit with Airflow owning retries, trigger rule all_success, a pipeloom_finalize task with all_done, and rid = af- plus 16 hex of sha256(dag_id + Airflow run_id), stable across task retries. With emit_assets, each model task declares Asset outlets.
  • DATABRICKS mode uses (b). A deferrable launch task finds or creates the job and calls run-now with pipeloom_run_id = rid, or repair if a failed run exists for rid. Each model gets a deferrable sensor that mirrors the state of its task_key.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One job definition however the run is triggered, and repair stays in Databricks.
  • Airflow task retries of a sensor only re-poll. Reruns go through launch.
  • Polling load is about one call per sensor per interval, with a configurable interval and an optional shared poll cache.
  • The shared artifact store for LOCAL and KUBERNETES modes is still open, with fsspec as the leading option (decide in 0.6).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0013: Run identity, idempotency, reruns
docs.text: Architecture: Section 17, ADR-0013 text

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A run can span several processes and orchestrator tasks, and tasks can be retried or repaired. Metadata, events and writes from all of them must join into one run, and a retry must not duplicate data.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• A fresh run_id per attempt. Simple, but splits one logical run into many.
  • A stable run_id with an attempt counter, derived deterministically by orchestrators.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• run_id is either caller-supplied or generated as YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ-<6 hex>, matching [A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}.
  • Orchestrators derive it deterministically: dbx-<job_run_id> or af-<hash>.
  • Orchestrator retries and repairs keep the run_id and increment the attempt.
  • Local pipeloom retry --from <run_id> creates a new run with parent_run_id, selecting result:fail+ (failed units plus their skipped descendants).
  • Writes are idempotent through the token <run_id>:<model>.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A cleared-and-rerun Airflow task continues the same pipeloom run.
  • Engines without idempotent writes declare idempotent_writes=False, and validation forbids retries on non-idempotent append (PLC505).
  • Run records go to the state store for history.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0014: Secrets by reference
docs.text: Architecture: Section 14, Security and secrets

docs.title: Context
docs.text: YAML files, manifests, events and artifacts are committed, logged and shared. Secret values must never end up in them.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Literal secrets in YAML. Convenient, and unsafe.
  • Environment variables only. Safe, but no integration with platform secret stores.
  • References resolved at runtime through providers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Secrets by reference.

  • Fields whose names match secret patterns accept only ${secret:...} or ${env:...}. A literal is PLS104.
  • ${secret:<provider>/<path>} resolves at runtime inside the executing process through the pipeloom.secret_providers group. Providers: env and file (core, mode-checked), databricks (secret scopes), airflow (connections and variables).
  • The manifest, events and artifacts store only the references. Resolved values are registered with the redaction filter (ADR-0010).
  • Discovery never imports plugins until a config names them. PIPELOOM_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD exists for locked-down hosts.
  • Grants are declared in YAML and applied by the catalog. pipeloom never escalates privileges.
  • Supply chain: trusted publishing (OIDC) with PEP 740 attestations, actions pinned by commit SHA, no pull_request_target workflows, integration secrets only in protected environments, and private vulnerability reporting through SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The compile-time manifest is safe to share. Secrets exist only in the running process.
  • ${secret:...} is not resolved at compile time, so a bad reference shows up at run time (or in --preflight).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0015: Python 3.11 or newer; click CLI; pydantic v2; hatchling; mypy strict
docs.text: Architecture: Section 17, ADR-0015 text, and section 18

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A new public project started in late 2026 must pick a Python floor and a base toolchain. Python 3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Python floor: 3.10 (reaches end of life in October 2026) or 3.11.
  • CLI: click (click>=8.2, for CliRunner to expose result.stderr; the 0.0.2 skeleton depended on click>=8.1).
  • Config models: pydantic v2, which also exports the JSON Schema (section 4).
  • Build backend: hatchling.
  • Types: mypy in strict mode.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Python 3.11 or newer, click for the CLI, pydantic v2 for config models, hatchling as the build backend, and mypy --strict in CI. CI runs Python 3.11 to 3.14 on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Code may use 3.11 features, and users on 3.10 cannot install pipeloom.
  • The package had one runtime dependency (click) at 0.0.2. From 0.1 the CLI needs click>=8.2, and the runtime also depends on pydantic>=2.12 and PyYAML>=6.0.2.
  • pyproject.toml and CI follow this ADR.
  • While the repo was private, CI ran one Windows and one macOS job on 3.12 only, to save macOS minutes. The full matrix returned when the repo went public on 2026-11-02.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0016: Versioning, release, plugin API version
docs.text: Architecture: Section 15 (Release) and section 6 (Plugin API version)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Several distributions ship from one repository, and several contracts evolve at different speeds: the package, the plugin protocol, the config format and the manifest, event and run_results schemas.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Lockstep versions for first-party distributions during 0.x, with one tag. Simple releases. Plugin-only fixes still bump every distribution.
  • Independent versions per distribution. Precise, but more release work and a larger compatibility matrix while the API is moving.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• SemVer per distribution, with lockstep versions for first-party distributions during 0.x and one tag vX.Y.Z.
  • The tag workflow checks that the tag equals the version, builds, then publishes to PyPI by trusted publishing, then creates the GitHub release with notes from CHANGELOG.md (Keep a Changelog).
  • Each distribution publishes from its own job and its own GitHub environment: pypi for the core and pypi-<plugin> for each plugin (pypi-polars, pypi-pandas, pypi-spark, pypi-databricks, pypi-airflow). PyPI accepts only one pending trusted publisher per owner, repository, workflow and environment, so new plugin projects cannot share one environment. Amended on 2026-11-04 after PyPI rejected a second pending publisher for pypi; ADR-0023 has the job layout.
  • config_version, the manifest and event schema versions, and the plugin API version are versioned separately.
  • pipeloom.plugins.API_VERSION = (MAJOR, MINOR), independent of the package version. MINOR covers additive changes. MAJOR covers breaking protocol changes. The core accepts plugins with the same MAJOR and MINOR not above its own, otherwise it raises PLU001.
  • Before 1.0 the plugin API is 0.x and any minor may break. Plugin API 1.0 ships with pipeloom 1.0.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plugin authors can target a plugin API version instead of a package version.
  • Lockstep versioning means plugin-only fixes bump every distribution during 0.x.
  • At 1.0, config_version: 1, the plugin API 1.0, and the manifest, event and run_results schemas v1 are declared stable.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amended by ADR-0017: while the plugin API major is 0 the versions must match exactly.

docs.title: ADR-0017: Plugin spec, built-in plugins and the exact plugin API gate
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 6, Plugin system and plugin API version

Amends ADR-0004 and ADR-0016.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Building the first plugins showed gaps in the contracts those ADRs describe:

  • A spec that only carries name and kind cannot say which group it belongs to, so a mismatch between an entry point and the spec behind it goes unnoticed. L5 also needs to read an engine's capabilities without building the engine, and plugins list needs a one-line description.
  • Built-in plugins (the memory engine, the naming strategies, the env secret provider) must work when third-party autoload is off, and they must not cost an import when nobody names them. Registering them as entry points of the core distribution would make them depend on how the package was installed.
  • ADR-0016 accepts a plugin whose minor version is at most the core's. Before 1.0 any minor may break, so that rule would accept plugins built for an older, different protocol.
  • Loading can fail in more ways than PLU001 and PLU002 cover.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Built-ins as core entry points. Uniform with third-party plugins, but they vanish when autoload is off or the metadata is missing, for example in a vendored or zipped install.
  • Built-ins imported eagerly. Simple, but every command pays for every built-in, and the memory engine pulls in sqlite3.
  • A lazy in-code table of module:attr strings. Nothing is imported until a config names the kind.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• PluginSpec gains group, capabilities and description. The fields are now name, kind, group, api_version, factory, config_model, compatible_engines, capabilities and description. capabilities is static data: EngineCapabilities for engines, StateStoreCapabilities for state stores, None otherwise. Spec modules must not import heavy libraries at module level, so reading a spec never loads an engine library.
  • Built-in plugins come from pipeloom.plugins.builtin.BUILTINS, a table of module:attr strings by group and kind. They are listed with source builtin and the distribution pipeloom. They stay available when PIPELOOM_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1, which only skips third-party entry points. --plugin module:attr always loads, and its module is imported during discovery because the group and kind are only known from the spec.
  • While the plugin API major version is 0, a plugin's api_version must equal the core's exactly, otherwise PLU001. From 1.0 the ADR-0016 rule applies: same major, minor not above the core's.
  • New code PLU003 covers every other load failure: the module cannot be imported, the entry point does not resolve to a PluginSpec, or the spec's group or kind differs from the entry point that registered it.
  • A kind provided by two entries in one group, built-ins included, is PLU002 once a config names it. pipeloom plugins list flags it and exits 1.
  • Naming blocks use kind like every other plugin block: naming: {kind: per_user, schema: dev}.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Built-ins cost nothing until used, and behave the same in every install layout.
  • A third-party plugin cannot silently replace a built-in kind; it has to use another name.
  • Plugin authors must rebuild against each 0.x core release. That matches ADR-0016's promise that any 0.x minor may break.
  • Exact matching rejects a plugin that would still work, which is a deliberate trade until the protocols settle.
  • The filesystem catalog is registered now with its options model, and its implementation arrives in 0.2.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0018: Events in 0.1: invocation events, nullable run id, jsonl on stderr
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 11

Amends ADR-0010.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0010 defines the event stream for runs. In 0.1 there is no run yet, but every command (validate, schema export, plugins list, later compile) should report through the same bus, so diagnostics, logs and artifacts do not grow a second path. A few details of the envelope also need fixing before any consumer depends on them.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Keep printing diagnostics directly and add events with runs in 0.2. Two paths to maintain, and the console format would change later.
  • Route every command through the bus now, with a small set of invocation events.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every command is an invocation with its own invocation_id and an event bus.

  • run_id is nullable. Outside a run it is null.
  • New event types: invocation.started, invocation.completed and plan.compiled. plan.compiled is the compile-only form of run.compiled (project, target, plan hash, unit counts, selection). diagnostic, artifact.written and sink.disabled are used as in ADR-0010.
  • The envelope has a schema key with the value pipeloom.event/1, so a line of jsonl identifies itself.
  • data is always a JSON object.
  • A command collects what it finds and emits at the end, in this order: invocation.started, diagnostics (sorted by file, line, column, code), plan.compiled and artifact.written if any, invocation.completed.
  • --log-format text|json (PIPELOOM_LOG_FORMAT) picks the terminal sink: console (text) or jsonl to stderr (json). Sinks listed under events.sinks in pipeloom.yml are added after the project loads and binds. Stdout stays for command results.
  • console and jsonl are built-in sink plugins. failure_budget, buffered and buffer_size apply to every sink. The jsonl sink takes an optional path, relative to the project directory; without it the sink writes to stderr.
  • A sink that fails failure_budget times in a row is disabled (PLE401, a warning) and the other sinks receive sink.disabled. A sink that is still failing when the bus closes gets the same notice, so failures below the budget are not silent.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Scripts read machine output from stderr with --log-format json and command results from stdout.
  • Diagnostics are visible in events, so later sinks (files, lineage) get them without extra work.
  • Nothing is printed until a command ends, so a long command shows no progress. Runs in 0.2 emit as they go.
  • Redaction is in the bus, but nothing registers secret values until providers resolve secrets at run time.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0019: YAML dialect: PyYAML with YAML 1.2 core scalars
docs.text: Architecture: Section 4

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every config file is YAML, and users hit its sharp edges. YAML 1.1, which PyYAML implements by default, turns NO into a boolean (the Norway problem), reads 010 as octal and resolves bare dates to timestamps. Diagnostics also need the line and column of every key and value, and files can be hostile: duplicate keys, recursive aliases and alias expansion bombs must not hang or crash the tool.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• PyYAML as is. Zero extra work, but YAML 1.1 scalars silently change country codes and ids, and duplicate keys overwrite each other.
  • ruamel.yaml. Tracks marks and speaks YAML 1.2, but adds a dependency with its own quirks, and its round-trip data types leak into the models.
  • PyYAML with a YAML 1.2 core resolver and our own constructor. Keeps one small, well-known dependency and controls scalars, marks and limits.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
pipeloom parses with PyYAML and composes the node tree with a loader whose implicit resolvers are the YAML 1.2 core schema: only true and false are booleans, null, ~ and an empty value are null, integers may be decimal, 0o octal or 0x hex, and nothing resolves to a timestamp. country: NO stays a string.

Our own constructor walks the nodes. It records the mark of every key and value under its RFC 6901 pointer, reports duplicate keys as PLY002, supports merge keys (<<, with explicit keys winning and merged keys exempt from the duplicate check) and rejects non-string keys. It counts every constructed node, including those reached through aliases. A recursive alias, or an expansion above 100000 nodes, is PLY001. More than one document in a file is PLY001. Bytes that are not UTF-8 (a UTF-8 BOM is stripped) and characters YAML forbids are PLY003.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Configs behave the same on every machine, and Norwegian users can write NO.
  • Files that rely on YAML 1.1 booleans such as yes or on get strings, and pydantic's lax mode only converts the strings it knows.
  • Diagnostics point at exact lines and columns. A value that comes from an alias reports the mark of the anchor's definition.
  • The loader is a small amount of code we own and test. A move to another parser later only has to keep the LoadedDocument contract.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0020: Execution model in 0.2
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 8, Execution and scheduler

Amends ADR-0006, ADR-0007 and ADR-0010.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: 0.2 is the first release that runs plans. The scheduler, the executors and the unit events need one agreed shape before the model runner, the process executor and the console rendering are built on them.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• An executor config key. Flexible, but a second knob that can contradict boundary.
  • The boundary picks the executor. One setting, one meaning.
  • Multiprocessing for the process executor. Shares state implicitly and behaves differently per platform.
  • A subprocess that runs pipeloom run --select unit:<id>. Only argv crosses the boundary, so the same path works from an orchestrator.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The boundary picks the executor. boundary: process uses a thread pool and one engine session shared by the invocation; boundary: task starts a subprocess per unit. There is no executor key and no multiprocessing.
  • The scheduler is a ready-queue loop with no level barrier. Ready units sit in a heap ordered by (-downstream, unit_id), so a given completion order always yields the same start order. Parents outside the selection count as satisfied.
  • It talks to an Executor protocol: submit, a blocking wait_any, cancel (unused until 0.3) and shutdown. The thread executor and a simulated executor for tests implement it.
  • Unit states are checked against one transition table. queued -> skipped and queued -> cancelled exist besides the section 8 transitions, because a unit waits in the queue while a failure or a stop arrives. retrying, timed_out and running -> cancelled are in the table and unused until 0.3.
  • A failure skips every pending or queued descendant in topological order with reason upstream_failed and the failed unit id. --fail-fast skips every other pending or queued unit with reason fail_fast; running units finish. A stop request cancels pending and queued units and lets running units finish.
  • An internal error (a bug in the runner or executor, not a failed unit) stops dequeuing, drains the running units and is re-raised after the scheduler result is built.
  • The scheduler emits unit.queued, unit.skipped and unit.cancelled. The invocation that executes a unit emits unit.started, the terminal unit event and the model.* events. With boundary: task the child emits its own and the owning invocation forwards them, keeping the child's invocation id and sequence. Attempt files are written by the runner, and the child's attempt file is the authoritative result.
  • A unit invocation (--select unit:<id> only) takes no run lock, emits no run.* events and does not finalize.
  • The run lock is a lease (60 s, heartbeat every 20 s), not a process liveness check.
  • Refinements made with the process executor. A child gets PIPELOOM_PARENT_INVOCATION_ID and then opens only its stderr jsonl sink and its own run file sink, never the project's sinks. The parent relays every child event except invocation.* and diagnostic, and sinks that set forwarded = False (the run file sink) do not receive relayed events. In unit mode the scheduler does not announce unit.queued, unit.skipped or unit.cancelled; the owner does. A child that exits without an attempt file is reported by the parent as PLX106: it writes the failed attempt file at the number above the pre-launch maximum and emits the one unit.failed event. A held run lock is PLX105 (holder, run and lease expiry). --expect-plan-hash is checked before any work (PLX103), and a manifest of another project or target, or one edited after it was written, is PLX107.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Scheduler events are deterministic for a given completion order; with one worker or the simulator the whole stream is.
  • Property tests run the scheduler on random graphs with the simulator and check the invariants.
  • The thread executor cannot stop a running unit. Cooperative cancellation, retries and timeouts come in 0.3 and change wait_any and cancel in an additive way.
  • Starting a subprocess per unit costs about a second per unit.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0021: Plugin API (0, 2)
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 5, Engine and catalog contracts

Amends ADR-0002 and ADR-0017.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: 0.2 is the first release that runs models. The 0.1 engine contract had no way to check what a Python model returned, to share one result between units, to create a view, to say which materializations an engine offers, or to tell whether a state store is visible to other processes. The model runner needs all of them, and the engine plugins (polars, pandas) are built against the same API.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Keep the 0.1 contract and let the runner work around it. The runner would guess at native types and could not reject a foreign return value with a useful error.
  • Add the missing pieces to the protocols. One additive change, and core, plugins and the memory engine move together.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The plugin API version becomes (0, 2). While the major version is 0 a plugin must match it exactly (ADR-0017), so every plugin is rebuilt for it. The change is additive:

  • Engine.version names the engine library's version and goes into run_results.json.
  • Engine.session(ctx, *, catalog) receives the catalog. A session is created once per invocation and must be thread-safe, because the thread executor shares it.
  • EngineSession.relation(native) checks a model's return value and wraps it in a Relation. It raises TypeError for a foreign type, which the runner reports as PLX101 with a hint.
  • EngineSession.persist(rel) returns an in-memory copy that later reads reuse. The runner calls it for an ephemeral model that more than one unit inlines.
  • EngineSession.create_view(target, query, inputs) creates or replaces a catalog view. inputs maps the aliases used in query to ReadSpecs; a persisted model is read as format table.
  • EngineCapabilities.materializations lists what the engine can store: table, view and ephemeral in 0.2. A model whose materialization is missing is PLC509, so incremental and intermediate are rejected until an engine declares them. Views keep PLC507 for engines without view support.
  • StateStoreCapabilities.shared says whether every process and task of a run sees the store. PluginSpec.capabilities holds either kind of capabilities.
  • ReadSpec.format may be table, a table of the catalog named by ReadSpec.table.
  • The state store records runs and unit attempts (record_run, list_units) next to watermarks and locks.
  • A view must be a SQL model that inlines no ephemeral model, because the query is stored as written (PLP409).

The runner does not call EngineSession.filter_since, max_value or cancel; they stay for 0.3.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plugins built for (0, 1) fail with PLU001 until they are updated.
  • The memory engine implements the whole contract, including views, so the contract suites can run against it.
  • The runner has one place (_to_frame_api) where Narwhals frames will be wired in, for engines that declare portable.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0022: Filesystem table format
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 5, Engine abstraction

Amends ADR-0008 and ADR-0013.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The polars and pandas engines write files, and a rerun of the same run id must not write twice (ADR-0013). Plain files give no atomic multi-file publish and no place to remember which idempotency tokens were applied. Views also need a home on a catalog that has no SQL engine of its own.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Glob the table directory. Simple, but a half-written part file or a crash between two writes is visible to readers.
  • Adopt Delta or Iceberg. Solves it, but adds a heavy dependency for a default catalog.
  • A small commit file next to the parts. One atomic rename publishes a new file set, and the same file holds the token log.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A table is a directory <root>/<schema>/<name>/ with part files part-<uuid12>.<ext> and _pipeloom/commit.json. The catalog name of a target is ignored.
  • The commit file is written to commit.json.<uuid>.tmp and moved with os.replace (retried on Windows). Readers use the files the commit lists, never a directory listing. A part file no commit lists is invisible.
  • The commit carries a format version ("schema": "pipeloom.fs_table/1"; a reader rejects any other value), a commit counter, the file names, the logical columns, row and byte totals and the last 100 applied idempotency tokens with their write results. The stored result is the writer's result with target_version set to the commit version (and bytes_written filled from the part files when the writer left it empty), so a replay is identical to the first write. A write with a token already in the log returns the stored result and writes nothing. This is the only catalog that offers idempotent writes; polars and pandas declare idempotent_writes=True because they write through it.
  • Overwrite commits the new files and then deletes part-* files not in the commit, best effort. Append lists the old files plus the new ones. An overwrite with no rows still writes one file, so the schema survives in columns.
  • A view is a commit of kind view with no files and a ViewDefinition (the SQL and its inputs). Catalog inputs store the TargetRef, never a path. Reading a view runs the SQL again. Only SQL models become views (PLP409).
  • There is no commit lock: one model writes a target at a time. Merge and replace_partitions can add a lock file and per-partition files under a new format version without breaking readers of version 1.
  • Narwhals enters the core as a dependency used by pipeloom.engine.portable alone, through narwhals.stable.v2. An import-linter contract keeps every other module from importing it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• External tools that glob a table directory may see part files of an unfinished write; they should read through the commit file.
  • os.replace is weak on network file systems, and an orphan part file from a crash survives until the next overwrite.
  • A schema or token change that older readers cannot parse needs a new format version.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0023: Multi-distribution release
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 17, ADR-0005 text

Amends ADR-0005 and ADR-0016.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: 0.2 adds the first plugin distribution, pipeloom-polars, to the uv workspace, and pipeloom-pandas follows. One tag must publish all of them at the same version. PyPI creates a project from a pending trusted publisher on the first upload, and a pending publisher does not reserve the name. Whether one pending publisher can serve several projects in one workflow run is unconfirmed.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• One publish step for a flat dist/. Simple, but one missing publisher fails the whole upload and gives no control over order.
  • A separate workflow or job per distribution. Clear failures, but the tag fans out into jobs that each need the environment approval.
  • One job with one publish step per distribution, core first, each with skip-existing. A failure stops at the broken step, earlier steps stay published and a rerun skips what is already on PyPI.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Every distribution has the same version (lockstep, ADR-0016), each plugin depends on pipeloom~=X.Y.0, and the root extras pin pipeloom-<name>==X.Y.Z. tools/versions.py check [--tag vX.Y.Z] verifies this, the release workflow runs it before building, and bump X.Y.Z rewrites the lines and runs uv lock. The root extra and the plugin's dependency on the root form a cycle; uv lock accepts it.
  • The release builds each distribution with uv build --package <name> -o dist/<name>/. Each distribution has its own publish job and GitHub environment (pypi for the core, pypi-<plugin> for a plugin) with id-token: write only, packages-dir: dist/<name>/, attestations: true and skip-existing: true. Plugin jobs wait for the core job and run only when their distribution was built. The GitHub release runs after every publish job that ran and attaches every wheel and sdist.
  • Amended on 2026-11-04: the first layout used one job with one step per distribution in the pypi environment. PyPI accepts only one pending trusted publisher per owner, repository, workflow and environment, and rejected a second plugin on pypi, so the steps became jobs with an environment each.
  • A pending publisher is created for each new distribution right before tagging (checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md): project name, Owner emanuel-luis, Repository pipeloom, Workflow release.yml, Environment pypi-<plugin>. A missing one fails its own job with invalid-pending-publisher; fix it and re-run the failed jobs.
  • PEP 639 forbids .. in license-files, so each plugin directory holds its own copy of LICENSE and NOTICE.
  • CI builds every distribution with uv build --all-packages, installs the core wheel alone in a clean venv, then all wheels in a second one and runs pipeloom plugins list --check and a smoke project on polars.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A plugin name stays unclaimed until its pending publisher is used, so someone else could register it first; the checklist narrows that window to the release itself.
  • If PyPI accepts only one pending publisher per token, the per-step layout limits the damage to the steps after it, and a rerun finishes the job.
  • The LICENSE and NOTICE copies can drift; the release review compares them.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0024: Plugin API (0, 3)
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 5, Engine and catalog contracts

Amends ADR-0002 and ADR-0021.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: 0.3 adds incremental models, merge and replace_partitions, schema-change policies, expectations with quarantine, retries, timeouts and cancellation. The (0, 2) contract has no way to filter by a watermark with a strict bound, to count quality violations, to split dropped rows, to align a frame to a chosen schema, to look up an idempotency token before reading anything, to tag work for cancellation, or to classify an error as retryable. It also cannot say what a write changed beyond row counts.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Let the core do the work on rows. The core would pull data out of the engine, which defeats lazy and remote engines and breaks the rule that the core never looks inside a relation.
  • Engines count, the core judges. Engines compute raw counts and aggregates over their own frames; pass or fail, ratios, events and diagnostics stay in the core. One pure-Python reference defines the semantics and the contract suite compares every engine with it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The plugin API version becomes (0, 3). While the major version is 0 a plugin must match it exactly (ADR-0017), so every plugin is rebuilt for it.

EngineSession gains:

  • filter_since(rel, column, lower, *, inclusive=True): the strict form serves a watermark without lookback.
  • evaluate(rel, checks) returning QualityCounts and apply_drops(rel, checks, *, quarantine) returning DropResult. Both need the new capability quality; an engine without it raises NotImplementedError and L5 will reject expectations on it.
  • align(rel, schema): select in schema order, add missing columns as typed nulls, cast to the types. The core decides the final table schema; the engine only applies it.
  • applied_token(target, token): the stored WriteResult with skipped=True, or None. The runner can skip read, body and write when a token was already applied.
  • unit_scope(unit_id), is_transient(exc) and an active cancel(unit_id).
  • max_value returns plain Python values, never numpy or pandas scalars.

WriteConfig gains partition_by, update_condition (engine dialect, source. and target. qualifiers, a bare name means source), deletes (DeleteSpec), columns (the final schema chosen by the core) and commit_meta. WriteResult gains skipped and commit_meta; its other fields already carried the architecture names. commit_meta is stored with the token and echoed on replay, so a replayed write returns the watermark and quality summary of the original attempt.

New types: ColumnChange, SchemaDiff, ExpectationSpec, QualityCounts, QuarantineMeta, DropResult, plus can_widen and diff_schemas. Errors live in pipeloom.engine.errors: TransientError (raise it to force a retryable failure), CommitConflict (a transient error for table commit races) and WriteKeyError (a missing key column or a duplicate merge key, reported as PLM206).

Row-check semantics are fixed for all engines: a check passes on null input except not_null; NaN counts as null; range bounds are inclusive; regex is an unanchored search; accepted_values compares exactly; expr true passes, false fails, null passes. Aggregates see only the relation passed in. pipeloom.testing.reference implements all of it over plain rows, and the contract suite compares each engine with it.

The memory engine implements the whole contract (merge, replace_partitions, quality, cancel, incremental materialization). The polars and pandas engines move to (0, 3) and implement the whole contract except cancel: align, applied_token, unit_scope, is_transient, filter_since, evaluate and apply_drops. They declare quality, merge, replace_partitions and the incremental materialization. Their cancel stays a no-op (cancel=False).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plugins built for (0, 2) fail with PLU001 until they are updated.
  • An engine that cannot cancel keeps cancel=False and no-ops.
  • Widening rules (can_widen) are part of the contract, so the core can decide schema changes without asking the engine.
  • Dialect strings (expr, update_condition) are the only engine-specific text; contract cases keep to a common subset.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0025: Filesystem tables v2
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 5, Engine abstraction

Amends ADR-0022.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Merge and replace_partitions need to read the committed table, compute a new one and publish it, and two writers must not both succeed from the same starting point. Format /1 has no lock, does not know which rows a part file holds and keeps no partition values, so replacing a partition would mean reading every file. ADR-0022 left room for a lock file and per-partition files under a new format version.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Keep /1 and rewrite the whole table for every strategy. No format change, but replace_partitions reads and rewrites data it does not touch.
  • Delta or Iceberg. Solves it, but is the heavy dependency ADR-0022 rejected for the default catalog.
  • Format /2: per-file row counts and partition values, a commit lock and an expected version. Small, and /1 tables stay readable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The commit file declares "schema": "pipeloom.fs_table/2". A reader accepts /1 and /2 and rejects anything else. A /1 table is read as a table whose files have unknown rows and no partition values, and its next commit writes /2. Nothing rewrites old part files.
  • file_info maps each part file to FsFile(rows, bytes, partition). Partition keys are computed natively, never from a Python round trip: a timestamp is its epoch in nanoseconds, a decimal its text, a float its value with NaN as null, a date or time its text, and rows are grouped by those exact columns. The stored JSON value is a normalized text of the same key: ISO text for timestamps (UTC, nine fractional digits), a decimal without trailing zeros, null for null and NaN. A key therefore keeps matching after a lossless widening (decimal scale, timestamp unit, int to float); float32 to float64 is the one widening that does not. The write guards that the parts add up to the frame's row count. partition_by on the commit names the columns the values belong to. When a write changes partition_by, the old files keep no partition values and are treated as unknown.
  • With partition_by set, every strategy writes one part file per distinct partition tuple (null is a value). An empty batch writes one empty file without a partition.
  • A commit takes _pipeloom/commit.lock, created with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, with a 30 second lease. An expired lock is taken over by renaming it away first, the same way the JSON state store does. Under the lock the commit compares the committed version with expected_version (0 for a table that does not exist) and publishes with one atomic replace of commit.json. A held lock or a version mismatch raises CommitConflict, a TransientError. There is no wait or retry in the table; the scheduler owns retries.
  • Merge and replace_partitions are read-modify-write. The engine reads the committed table through the commit schema (FsTable.read_aligned), aligns it and the batch to the final schema, and computes the result with the portable Narwhals code (merge_frames, replace_partition_frames). Merge writes the result as an overwrite. In 0.3 a merge rewrites the whole table; a per-partition rewrite is a later optimization. Replace_partitions drops the files whose partition is in the batch and adds the batch files in one append commit, without reading data. Files with no partition values are read, filtered and rewritten. rows_deleted comes from file_info.rows.
  • An empty merge batch commits a new version with the same files. An empty replace_partitions batch changes no files. Both record the token. A merge or replace_partitions into a table that does not exist writes the batch as a new table.
  • The shared write logic lives in pipeloom.builtins.fs_write; each engine supplies a small FrameOps object (collect, read a file, align, concat, write, evaluate the update condition in its own dialect).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Two writers on one table no longer corrupt it: the second one fails with a transient conflict and reruns from the new version.
  • Merge cost grows with table size. Overwrite still deletes every part-* file the new commit does not list, so a concurrent writer's uncommitted file can be removed; its commit then fails or is discarded.
  • A stale lock from a crashed writer blocks commits for up to 30 seconds.
  • Partition pruning on read is not implemented; the values are recorded so it can be.
  • Splitting a frame filters once per partition (O(partitions x rows)) because Narwhals has no single-pass split; each part is written and released in turn.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0026: Schema-change policy
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 9, Incremental processing, write strategies, schema change

Amends ADR-0008.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: write.on_schema_change had four named policies and no rules. A batch can add, drop or retype columns, and the answer depends on what the strategy does with the rows already in the table. The core must decide the final schema without asking the engine, and every engine must end up with the same table.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Let each engine decide. Simple for plugins, but the same model would evolve differently on polars and on the memory engine.
  • The core decides, the engine applies. One pure function picks the final schema from the target schema, the batch schema, the policy and the strategy. Engines only align a frame to a schema and read old data through the table's current schema.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The core decides. pipeloom.runtime.schema_policy.resolve_columns(policy, target, batch, *, strategy, full_refresh) returns the final schema, a SchemaDiff and an action (applied, ignored, rejected, replaced or none). The runner passes the final schema as WriteConfig.columns and aligns the batch with EngineSession.align first.

The policy applies only when the strategy keeps existing rows (append, merge, replace_partitions), the target exists, and the run is not a full refresh. Overwrite, full refresh and a first build use the batch schema; a non-empty diff is still reported, with action replaced.

  • fail: any change is PLM202.
  • ignore: the final schema is the target's. The batch is aligned to it: extra columns dropped, missing ones filled with nulls, values cast to the target types. A cast that fails is PLM201.
  • append_new_columns: the target's columns followed by the added ones, in batch order and nullable. Removed columns stay. A type change is PLM202.
  • sync_all_columns: the batch's columns. A type change is accepted only when can_widen(target, batch); otherwise PLM202.

A batch whose types differ from the target only by a lossless widening of the target type (diff_schemas reports no change) is cast up to the target's types under every policy.

Widening follows can_widen: integer to a wider integer or to float64, float32 to float64, decimals that keep every digit, finer timestamp units with the same zone, and the null type to anything.

No policy may drop a key or fill it with nulls: a row-keeping write whose batch lacks a unique_key or partition_by column is a write key error (PLM206) before any alignment. A full refresh turns append, merge and replace_partitions into overwrite.

Every non-empty diff emits model.schema_changed with relation, policy, action and changes, and is copied to schema_changes[] of the unit's run_results row (each change carries its action). A rejected change is emitted at warning level before the unit fails. The console prints one line per event. Architecture section 9 named the event schema.changed; section 11 and the code use model.schema_changed.

Tables with files, such as the filesystem catalog, read every committed file through the table's current schema, so append and widening never rewrite old files. An engine that cannot do that leaves EngineHarness.schema_on_read false and the contract matrix skips the cells that write a changed schema. The memory, polars and pandas engines all set it to true.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One matrix in EngineContract (4 policies, 4 kinds of change, 3 strategies) checks the final schema and rows of every engine against the reference.
  • A narrower batch type never fails a run; it is widened silently to the target.
  • Dropping a column with sync_all_columns also drops its old values on strategies that rewrite rows (merge, replace_partitions); on files it only hides them from readers.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0027: Incremental models
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 9, Incremental processing, write strategies, schema change

Amends ADR-0008.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0008 named the watermark and the compare-and-swap but left open how a unit starts without a watermark, what a retry commits, how types are matched, and who owns the lookback arithmetic. Two things can go wrong between the write and the swap: the process can die, and new input can arrive before the retry. A retry that reads the input again would then commit a watermark that covers rows it never wrote.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Recompute on retry. Simple, but the retried batch can differ from the written one, so the watermark can jump over rows.
  • Store the watermark with the write token. The write records the watermark it intends to commit in its commit metadata. A retry with the same token skips read, body and write and commits that stored value.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The watermark is stored with the token. pipeloom.runtime.incremental holds the logic: resolve reads the state, next_watermark picks the value, commit swaps it, and to_meta and from_meta carry it through WriteConfig.commit_meta and WriteResult.commit_meta.

The runner checks EngineSession.applied_token before it does any work. A replayed token emits model.written with skipped: true, rebuilds the schema fields and the watermark from the stored metadata, and goes straight to the swap. Otherwise the unit resolves the watermark, reads the input filtered, runs the body, computes the batch maximum on the filtered input, writes with the intended watermark in the commit metadata, and then swaps. Nothing that can be cancelled sits between a finished write and its swap.

Rules:

  • A unit is incremental when the materialization is incremental, the target exists, the run is not a full refresh, and a watermark exists. ctx.is_incremental, ctx.watermark and ctx.lower_bound are set only then.
  • With watermark_source: state and no stored watermark but an existing target, the watermark is seeded from max(column) of the target and watermark_seeded: target goes to warnings[]. With watermark_source: target the state store is never written.
  • Types are compared by family: timestamp with a zone, timestamp without one, date, integer, decimal, float, string. A stored watermark of another family than the input column is PLM205, as is a missing column.
  • lookback: 0 filters with column > w. A lookback above zero filters with column >= w - lookback for timestamps (seconds) and dates (whole days, rounded up); on any other family it is PLM205. There is no lookback on integers.
  • The new watermark is max(w, m) when incremental, where m is the batch maximum and may be below w or missing; otherwise it is m, and an empty first batch leaves the state alone. A full refresh commits m.
  • The swap is cas_watermark(expected, new) with expected as read at the start (none when seeded). Stores treat a stored value equal to new as success only when the same run stored it, which covers a replay after a crash between the swap and the attempt file; an equal value from another run is a lost race and fails. Any other mismatch is PLM203: the data is already written, the unit fails, and the error is permanent. StateStoreContract checks the rule.
  • Append with a lookback above zero reloads rows it already wrote; PLP410 warns and recommends merge.
  • plan.model.default_strategy gives the strategy of a model that sets none: append for incremental, overwrite otherwise. A full refresh writes append, merge and replace_partitions as overwrite. A first build keeps its strategy, because into an absent table every strategy writes the same rows and merge still checks its key.
  • PLC509 compares the materialization with EngineCapabilities.materializations; the memory, polars and pandas engines declare incremental.

New event state.watermark_committed (column, dtype, before, after, source, seeded). Rows of run_results gain is_incremental, watermark_before, watermark_after, rows_updated and rows_deleted values.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A retry with the same run id commits exactly the original batch's watermark, even when new rows arrived in between. This also holds in unit mode.
  • The commit metadata grows by a small JSON object per incremental write.
  • The batch maximum is computed on the filtered input, so a lazy engine scans it twice.
  • A first build that fails the merge key check does so on the first run, not the second.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0028: Expectation evaluation
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 10, Data quality

Amends ADR-0009.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Expectations have three actions (warn, drop, fail) and two families of check: row checks and aggregate checks. Every engine must count the same violations, and the run must report them the same way, or a model changes meaning when its engine changes.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Engines judge. Each engine returns pass or fail. Ratios, messages and events would then differ per engine.
  • Engines count, the core judges. Engines return raw counts and aggregate values. The core decides pass or fail, the drop ratio, PLQ301 and the events.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Engines count, the core judges (pipeloom.quality.judge). EngineSession.evaluate returns the total, violating rows per row check, rows violating at least one drop check, and aggregate values. apply_drops splits the rows. A pure-Python reference (pipeloom.testing.reference) defines the semantics and the contract suite compares every engine against it.

Row checks: a null input passes (SQL CHECK semantics) except for not_null; NaN counts as null; range bounds are inclusive; regex is an unanchored search in the common subset of Rust regex and re; accepted_values compares exactly. An expr is an engine-dialect string: true passes, false fails, null passes. Float columns have NaN turned into null before it is evaluated. What it may contain depends on the engine, and it never runs code:

  • polars: a SQL expression for pl.sql_expr (column names, literals, comparison, boolean and arithmetic operators, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, and the SQL functions polars supports). It sees the columns only.
  • pandas: a restricted Python expression for DataFrame.eval(engine="python"). Only column names, literals, comparison, and, or, not, &, |, ~, arithmetic, in and not in with a tuple or list are accepted. @name, function and method calls, attribute access, subscripts, comprehensions and conditional expressions are rejected before evaluation, and the evaluation gets no local or global names (a config file must not run code). A rejected expression is PLQ302. The same rule applies to a merge update_condition. A pandas frame backed by numpy floats cannot hold a null, so there a NaN compares as false.
  • memory: a sqlite expression over the row's columns.

regex needs a string column; any other type is PLQ302, because engines render non-strings differently.

Aggregate checks (unique, row_count, freshness) see only the batch, after the drops. For an incremental model that is the new rows, not the table. unique counts rows minus distinct keys and leaves out rows with a null key part. Freshness is now - max(column) computed by the core with the run's clock; a naive timestamp reads as UTC and an all-null column fails. An aggregate check cannot drop (PLP403).

Row counts are taken on the full output, so a failed drop check is still visible. The runner persists a lazy relation first (cached: true in the event), counts, drops if a drop check failed, then counts the aggregates on what is kept. When nothing can drop, one evaluate call counts everything.

A failed check with action fail, or a drop ratio above quality.max_drop_ratio, fails the unit with PLQ301 before it writes. The counts are still recorded: model.quality_evaluated, and expectations[], rows_dropped, rows_quarantined and warnings[] in run_results. Warnings keep the unit succeeded and print WARN lines on the console. An unknown column or an expr the engine rejects is PLQ302.

Quarantine: with quality.quarantine the dropped rows are appended to <target>__quarantine under the token <run_id>:<model>#quarantine, so a replay writes them once. rows_quarantined is 0 until that write has committed: a unit that fails with PLQ301 or on a rejected main schema reports no quarantined rows. The table has the model columns plus _pipeloom_run_id (string), _pipeloom_failed (list of the failing drop-check names, in declaration order) and _pipeloom_ts (timestamp[us, UTC]). On a csv catalog _pipeloom_failed is JSON text in a string column. Its schema policy is append_new_columns: new model columns are added and removed ones stay, so a changed model output keeps working. A column that changes type incompatibly is the one thing it cannot absorb: the unit fails with PLM202 naming the quarantine relation (a model.schema_changed event for that relation, schema_changes[] of the model untouched), before the main table is written. Any other quarantine write error is PLM201 naming the quarantine relation. The write happens after the schema policy accepted the main write and just before it.

Static checks: PLP411 (expectations on a view or ephemeral model, declared by the model itself), PLP412 (<model>__quarantine is also a model in the same schema), PLC510 (engine without the quality capability).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every engine reports the same counts; the dialect strings are the one place engines may differ.
  • A model with a failed fail-expectation leaves its target and its quarantine untouched.
  • Quarantine warnings are appended to warnings[]; they never replace warnings recorded earlier in the unit.
  • The memory JSON table store writes dates and datetimes as text, so a quarantine table kept in it cannot be appended to by a second run (the schema reads back as string). Real catalogs keep the types.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0029: Retries, timeouts and cancellation
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 8, Execution

Amends ADR-0006 and ADR-0020.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A unit can fail for reasons that pass on their own (a dropped connection, a table lock), run for too long, or be stopped with the run. 0.2 had the states for this but no behavior: a failed unit stayed failed, a hung unit hung the run, and an executor could not stop anything.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Retry inside the runner. Simple, but a process executor would then retry inside the child, where the parent cannot see it, and an external orchestrator would retry twice.
  • Retry in the owner of the schedule. The scheduler (the parent for the process executor) retries; a unit invocation under an orchestrator never does.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Retries belong to whoever schedules the unit. Scheduler keeps a retry heap and drives time from clock.monotonic() and Executor.wait_any(timeout); it never sleeps. A failed attempt with retries left moves RUNNING to RETRYING, emits unit.retrying and holds no worker slot while it waits. --select unit:... runs with retries=0; the child of a process executor is such an invocation.

Classification (pipeloom.runtime.retry.classify), in order: TransientError anywhere in the cause chain (depth 10); the engine's is_transient opinion; ConnectionError or TimeoutError in the chain; in the read, write and state phases any OSError except FileNotFoundError, PermissionError (but a Windows sharing violation, winerror 32 or 33, is transient), IsADirectoryError, NotADirectoryError and FileExistsError; PLX106 (a child that died without a result) is transient. Everything else is permanent. PLQ301, PLQ302, PLM202, PLM203, PLM205 and PLM206 are always permanent. retry_on: transient (the default) retries transient failures only; retry_on: any retries every failed attempt, quality and schema failures included, which repeats deterministic failures and is documented as such.

Backoff: d = min(max(base, 300), base * 2**(n - 1)) and the wait is d * (0.5 + 0.5 * u) with u from random.Random(f"{run_id}:{unit_id}:{n}"), so delays are in [d/2, d], capped, and reproducible.

Timeouts are per attempt and are never retried: a timed-out unit is TIMED_OUT (PLX102), its descendants are skipped, and the run fails. The thread executor runs one daemon thread per attempt so a timed-out thread can be abandoned. It sets the attempt's CancelToken, calls EngineSession.cancel(unit_id) once, writes the timed_out attempt file itself (the thread may never return) and drops whatever the thread reports later. The runner checks the token at checkpoints (before reading, after the body, before the write and around the quarantine write) and never between the start of the table write and the end of the watermark swap. Cancellation is cooperative, so an abandoned polars or pandas thread can still commit after the verdict; this is the one place where the attempt file can say timed_out while data moved. The first terminal attempt file wins (write_json_once: a temp file linked, or renamed on Windows, to the target, which fails when it exists), and run.completed reports abandoned_threads. Finalize lets a scheduler TIMED_OUT or CANCELLED verdict win over a result written later and records late_result: <status> in warnings[].

The process executor starts each child in its own process group (CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP on Windows, start_new_session elsewhere) so a terminal Ctrl+C reaches only the owner. The child enforces the timeout itself through its thread executor; the parent's own deadline is timeout + cancel_grace, after which it kills the child and everything it started (killpg on POSIX, taskkill /T /F on Windows, both only while the child has not been reaped, so a reused pid is never signalled) and writes the timed_out attempt. After a child exits on POSIX the executor sweeps its process group, so a grandchild cannot keep the pipes open. Reader threads and shutdown joins are bounded, so a stuck child cannot hang the run. Windows has no job objects in 0.3: a grandchild of a child that exits on its own survives. A graceful stop is SIGTERM on POSIX and CTRL_BREAK_EVENT on Windows (CTRL_C_EVENT cannot target a process group), followed by a kill after cancel_grace. The executor records every Popen, so a test can check that none outlived the run. The parent emits unit.timed_out or unit.cancelled only when the child did not already forward one for that attempt.

A stop request (RunControl.request_stop) cancels pending, queued and retrying units, asks running units to stop, lets those that finish within cancel_grace keep their real result, and then marks the rest CANCELLED (PLX104). RETRYING -> CANCELLED is added to the transition table, and fail-fast cancels retrying units. The run emits one run.cancel_requested{signal, grace_s}, finishes with status cancelled and exits 130.

pipeloom run wires signals to a RunControl (cli/_signals.py, main thread only, previous handlers restored): SIGINT and SIGTERM on POSIX, SIGINT and SIGBREAK (Ctrl+Break) on Windows. The first signal requests a graceful stop, the second a hard stop that skips the grace, the third raises KeyboardInterrupt. Handlers only set flags; RunControl calls registered wakers (the scheduler registers executor.wake), so the install function takes no executor. A hard stop, or the end of the grace, abandons the thread attempts that are still alive (their attempt file is written as cancelled and their late result is dropped). A unit invocation (child process) handles the same signals, stops its unit and exits 130. cancel_grace is a setting (Duration, default 30s) and the flag --cancel-grace overrides it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A flaky read or write no longer fails a run; the cost is visible as unit.retrying events, one attempt file per attempt and retries_used in the result row.
  • A hung thread cannot be killed. It is abandoned and counted, and it ends with the process; a hung polars or pandas call can therefore outlive its unit.
  • Timeouts and delays are whole seconds in the config (Duration); the scheduler accepts fractions, so tests and API users can use shorter ones.
  • Executor changes shape: wait_any(timeout), cancel(handle, reason), wake() and has_terminal_event(handle). UnitHandle gains seq and attempt.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Spark engine of 0.4 needs three things from the core that plugin API (0, 3) does not give it. Delta makes a write idempotent with an application id and a monotonically increasing transaction version, so every invocation of a run must see the same start time. Spark does its work when the write happens, so cancellation tags must cover the read, the body, the checks and the write, not only the body. A state store that lives in the engine (0.4 adds one on Delta) needs the engine session before the run lock is taken. Large results shared between units also need a place that is not a catalog table. This ADR covers the first half of the change: the API, the run start time and the ordering. The intermediate materialization is covered in the second half below.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Derive the start time inside each engine. Every engine would pick its own clock reading, so two invocations of one run (process boundary, retries after a crash) would disagree and Delta would refuse or double-apply writes.
  • Resolve it once in the core and put it in the runtime context. One definition, recorded with the run, available to every engine.
  • Open the session after the lock, as in 0.3. Simple, but a state store that needs a session cannot take the lock.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Plugin API becomes (0, 4); during 0.x the match is exact, so the memory, polars and pandas engines move with the core. RuntimeContext gains run_started_at (timezone-aware UTC) and artifacts_root (an absolute POSIX path or URI). EngineSession gains write_intermediate(rel, ref, token) with IntermediateRef(run_id, model, location). CatalogCapabilities(views=True) joins EngineCapabilities and StateStoreCapabilities as a value of PluginSpec.capabilities; PLC507 also fires when the bound catalog declares views=False, and the filesystem catalog declares views=True.

run_started_at resolves in this order: a recorded start for the run id, then --run-started-at (environment PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT), then the clock at the start of the owning invocation. A unit invocation with neither has no start. The flag must carry a UTC offset and needs --run-id; both are usage errors (exit 2). A flag that disagrees with the recorded start is PLX108 (exit 2) and names both values; an equal value is accepted. The first invocation records the resolved value as the run's started_at, so later invocations, unit invocations under the process boundary and reused run ids all read the same instant.

execute_run opens the engine session before any state-store call (reading the run record, taking state.lock), and closes it after the lock is released, so a store that lives in the engine reuses the engine's session. The session therefore opens without the run start: ctx.run_started_at is None there.
