The runner fills the additive WriteConfig.run_started_at once the start is resolved, and an engine that needs a stable write version (a Delta txnVersion) reads it from WriteConfig, never from the session context. IntermediateRef.run_started_at carries it for intermediate writes, which have no WriteConfig. RuntimeContext.run_started_at stays for models. The Python API rejects a naive run_started_at and a value without run_id. The runner holds EngineSession.unit_scope from the first read of a unit to the end of its write, once per attempt; the scope that wrapped only the model body is gone.

docs.title: Intermediates (amends ADR-0007)
docs.text:
An intermediate model is a persisted unit. Its result goes to <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model> through session.write_intermediate(rel, IntermediateRef(run_id, model, location), token="<run_id>:<model>"), and consumers read it with ReadSpec("intermediate", location=...). The write always overwrites, and a repeated token writes nothing. run_results reports the location as the unit's relation_name. An intermediate cannot be incremental, use a strategy other than overwrite, or set partition_by (PLP413). The memory engine keeps JSON at the location; polars and pandas keep a filesystem table there. A Spark Connect server whose filesystem differs from the client's needs a shared artifacts root; a scratch schema is a later option.

artifacts.intermediate_ttl (default 1d, 0 allowed) bounds how long they live. Finalize calls cleanup_intermediates after it knows the run status, and records the TTL as run.intermediate_ttl in run_results.json. A TTL of 0 deletes only the current run's folder, and only when the run succeeded. Every other run is judged by the TTL it recorded itself, because targets share the artifacts root and may configure different TTLs. A run's last activity is the newest of its ended_at and the newest modification time under its whole run folder (the manifest is rewritten at each start and events grow during a run), so a resumed run that only replays its writes still counts as active. A run whose manifest.json is newer than its run_results.json is running again and is never deleted. A run without run_results.json (still running, or crashed) keeps its folder until it has been idle for max(ttl, 1h). A missing folder is fine, and a deletion error becomes an entry in run.warnings, never a failure.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Engines can derive idempotency keys from run_started_at without reading the clock. A run that finds the lock held now opens and closes one session first, a small cost the memory, polars and pandas engines do not notice. A flag from an orchestrator that differs from what a retried run recorded stops the run instead of silently using the other value. Plugins built for (0, 3) fail with PLU001.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0031: Spark engine
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 3, Packages

Amends ADR-0002 and ADR-0005.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: 0.4 adds a Spark engine. Spark differs from polars and pandas in ways that shape the plugin: pyspark is large (a 450 MB source distribution) and is already present, in its own version, on Databricks runtimes and with Databricks Connect; a session is a heavyweight object shared by every worker thread; work happens when an action runs, which is at the write; and a session can be a local JVM, a Spark Connect client or a session someone else owns.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Depend on pyspark. Simple, but installing a second pyspark breaks Databricks runtimes and Databricks Connect.
  • No hard dependency, extras for local use. The plugin depends on pipeloom only; the extra local brings pyspark and Delta.
  • Job groups or tags for cancellation. Job groups do not exist in Connect. Tags do: SparkSession.addTag and interruptTag in Connect, and SparkContext.addJobTag and cancelJobsWithTag in classic Spark. Classic SparkSession.addTag exists since 4.0 but did not tag the jobs of a DataFrame action in the 4.2 test run (interruptTag found nothing), so the engine uses the SparkContext calls there.
  • Session temp views or DataFrame binding for SQL aliases. Temp views live in the session, so two units that use one alias collide. spark.sql(query, **frames) binds DataFrames without a name in the session.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
pipeloom-spark depends only on pipeloom. The extra local is pyspark[connect]>=4.0.1,<4.3 and delta-spark>=4.1,<4.5, and pipeloom[spark] pulls pipeloom-spark[local]. The floor is pyspark 4.0.1; the upper bounds follow the newest Delta release that supports the Spark version. Connect-only clients may install pyspark-client instead.

The spec module imports no Spark library. The engine and catalog modules also import pyspark only inside functions, so a Databricks environment without extras loads them.

Sessions have four modes: local, connect, active and auto. Only a session the engine built is stopped. The engine sets no Spark conf on a session it did not build and none at run time on any session; conf applies when the engine builds the session, and conf with active is an error. Per-write settings are DataFrameWriter options, which take precedence over session conf.

SQL aliases are common table expressions over {keyword} fields that spark.sql binds to DataFrames, with the braces of the user's query doubled. A query with no aliases is passed unchanged, since Spark does not format a query that has no keywords.

Each unit adds one job tag for the length of its reads, body and write (a session tag on Connect, a job tag on classic), and cancel interrupts the jobs with that tag. An interrupt sent before the unit's first job exists finds nothing, so a short-lived thread repeats it until the unit's scope ends (at most a minute). persist registers the persisted frame with the current unit, which unpersists it when its scope exits; a memoized ephemeral persisted by its first consumer is recomputed by later consumers once that unit ends, which is correct and slower.

Two catalogs ship: delta_path (tables at <root>/<schema>/<name>, no metastore) and spark_catalog (names through the session catalog, with views). The engine binds its session to the catalog for the run.

Spark tests opt in with the test-only variable PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK=classic|connect, and skip when pyspark, java or a non-Windows host is missing. Classic and Connect run as two pytest invocations because they cannot share a process. CI has a spark job on Ubuntu with Java 17; it is not a required check until it has two green runs on main. The typecheck job installs the spark dependency group so the plugin is checked against the real pyspark types.

This release declares only what it implements: reads, SQL, cancel and the table and ephemeral materializations, with no write strategy. EngineContract write tests that did not name the overwrite strategy (test_metrics, test_two_threads_materialize_at_once) now require it, as the other write tests do.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Databricks and Databricks Connect users install pipeloom-spark without extras and keep their own pyspark.
  • A Spark session is never reconfigured behind the user's back; the cost is that conf cannot be changed per run.
  • Cancel is cooperative: it stops jobs, not Python code between jobs.
  • The first CI run downloads pyspark and, for Delta, jars from Maven; a Maven outage fails the job.
  • Delta writes, idempotency, quality and the state store build on this session and catalog layer in later releases.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0032: Delta writes and idempotency
docs.text:
Architecture: Section 9, Write strategies and idempotency

Amends ADR-0008 and ADR-0013.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Spark engine writes Delta tables. A write must be safe to repeat with the same token, must report row and byte metrics, and must follow the schema-change policy the core chose, on classic Spark, Spark Connect and Databricks. Two facts shape the design. The DeltaTable Python API is not usable on a Connect session without a server plugin. And Delta applies txnAppId and txnVersion to a MERGE only through session confs, which would leak into concurrent units that share the session.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• DeltaTable API for MERGE. Needs Delta Connect on the server; not portable.
  • Session confs for MERGE idempotency. Leaks to other units of the same session.
  • SQL MERGE INTO, then an empty append that carries the token. Portable, no session state.
  • Dynamic partition overwrite for replace_partitions. Legacy since Delta 4.3 and only fits physical partitions. replaceWhere works on partitioned and unpartitioned tables.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
All Delta statements are SQL text or DataFrameWriter options; no Spark conf is set. DESCRIBE HISTORY, DESCRIBE DETAIL and MERGE INTO run the same everywhere.

Token and version. txnAppId is pipeloom/<project>/<model>, with the suffix #quarantine or #intermediate for those writes. txnVersion is WriteConfig.run_started_at (or IntermediateRef.run_started_at) in epoch milliseconds, never read from the session context. userMetadata holds {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "token", "commit_meta", "result"?}}. Without a run start time, or with txn_guard: false, only the history check applies.

Idempotency. Every write first looks for its token in DESCRIBE HISTORY ... LIMIT 100 and returns the stored result with skipped=True. After a write that produced no commit carrying the token, the scan is repeated (a racing attempt may have won), then the full history; a token found nowhere means Delta refused the write because a later txnVersion already exists for this model, and the engine raises PLM207. The limits: a newer run, an overlapping run (--no-lock) or a host clock that ran behind trips the guard; txn_guard: false turns it off.

Claim commit. A MERGE carries no transaction, and a migration overwrite or a mergeSchema commit runs before the guarded write, so on their own they would land before the guard can refuse anything. When the guard applies, a write that needs any of them (every merge into an existing table, and any write that needs a migration) first makes an empty append carrying the real txnAppId and txnVersion and the userMetadata {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "claim": token}}. It has no token key, so the token scan and the metrics ignore it. If no claim for this token is then found (the scan window, then the full history), Delta refused the version and the engine raises PLM207 before any data changes; a claim found from an earlier attempt of the same token (a crash retry) lets the write continue, but only when no newer commit carries another token or claim of the same app id (scanning newest first). A later run that wrote the model in between voids the old claim, so the retry gets PLM207 instead of merging over that run's data. After a claim, the write and the token commit use the app id <app id>@<token> with version 1, which still keeps two attempts of the same token from both committing.

Strategies. - append: mode("append"), mergeSchema when the final columns add columns. - overwrite: mode("overwrite") with overwriteSchema, so any schema policy result is accepted. - replace_partitions: replaceWhere over the distinct partition tuples of the batch (above 10,000 tuples it fails and recommends merge). Null partitions use IS NULL or <=>. An empty batch writes only the token commit. - merge: the claim commit, SQL MERGE INTO (null keys never match, so they insert), then an empty append with the token, the <app id>@<token> transaction and the stored result. A crash between the commits is safe: the retry finds its own claim, re-running the MERGE with the same batch converges, and the token commit is the race guard. Soft deletes are counted with one join and moved from updated to deleted. A merge into a missing table is the first load, written as an append of the batch without its delete rows (hard or soft), as on the portable path.

Schema policy. The core decides the final columns. Added columns go in the write itself (mergeSchema; for merge, an empty mergeSchema append first, with no token). Removed or widened columns run one migration commit first: the table is read, aligned to the final columns and overwritten with overwriteSchema, its userMetadata marking migration_for, and its partitioning kept. Migration commits carry no txn options and no token, so they never count in the metrics; with the guard on, the claim commit before them takes the write version.

Metrics come from the commit history. DeltaMetrics.before_write returns the latest version and after_write sums operationMetrics over the versions after it that carry the token, plus the newest MERGE commit for a merge. The mapping is a pure function (metrics_to_result). It is plugin-internal: with one implementation there is no core MetricsProvider.

Views and intermediates. create_view (the spark_catalog catalog only) emits CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW with one CTE per alias over the physical table or path. write_intermediate overwrites a Delta path under the #intermediate app id.

PLM207 is a new code and permanent for retries. The core raises it for the new WriteRefusedError an engine may raise.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every write costs one DESCRIBE HISTORY before and one after, plus a schema read.
  • The MERGE commit of a write is found by position (the newest MERGE after the starting version): a concurrent MERGE on the same table can be mistaken for it in the metrics only.
  • Delta type widening and column mapping are not required.
  • A guarded MERGE costs one more commit (the claim), and so does a guarded write that needs a migration commit.
  • With the guard on, PLM207 is raised before any data changes, for every strategy.

docs.title: Deviations found while testing
docs.text:
• Delta skips an append of an empty DataFrame unless the commit carries a transaction. When the guard does not apply (no run start time, or txn_guard: false), an empty token commit gets an app id of its own, <app id>@<token> with version 1, so it is still recorded.
  • A table that saveAsTable creates does not keep the writer's userMetadata. The spark_catalog catalog therefore creates a missing table empty first, with no token, for append, merge (first load) and replace_partitions, and the tokened write is an ordinary write into it.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0008 keeps run state (watermarks, run and unit records, the run lock) behind the StateStore protocol, with a sqlite store for one machine and a JSON directory store for a shared volume. A Spark project often runs where neither fits: several drivers, or a cluster whose local disk is not shared and whose object store gives no atomic create or rename. Such a project already has Delta tables and a Spark session, and Delta commits are atomic with optimistic concurrency.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• One Delta table, MERGE for every mutation. One table holds every record kind; a single MERGE gives compare-and-set and lease taking, since Delta rejects a commit that conflicts with a concurrent one. Needs only the Delta SQL extension, so it works the same on classic Spark, Spark Connect and Databricks. Each call is a Spark job, so it is slower than sqlite.
  • One table per record kind. Mirrors the sqlite schema, but quadruples the tables to create, version and clean up, for no gain in atomicity.
  • The DeltaTable Python API. Routes to Delta Connect on a Connect session, which needs a server plugin (ADR-0032 rejects it for writes for the same reason).
  • An external database. Strong, but a new dependency and a new service to run.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The pipeloom-spark plugin adds the table state store (shared=True): one Delta table, partitioned by kind (watermark, run, unit, lock), addressed by catalog name (table) or by path (path), exactly one of the two. A row is found by (kind, key), where key is the canonical JSON array of the record's natural key. The data column holds the record in the core codec's JSON, so it reads back exactly; the other columns (project, run_id, status, owner, cas_key, expires_us and the other epoch-microsecond times) serve queries and MERGE conditions. The table property pipeloom.state.schema is 1; a higher value is refused with the same error as sqlite. It is created with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS; a lost creation race is ignored when the table is then readable.

Every insert or replace is one MERGE INTO <table> AS t USING {src} AS s ON t.kind = '<kind>' AND t.kind = s.kind AND t.key = s.key whose source is a one-row DataFrame from createDataFrame, so no record value is spliced into SQL text. The literal t.kind = '<kind>' (one of four fixed names) lets Delta prune to that kind's partition: without it the MERGE reads the whole table, and a unit record written by one worker conflicted with the run record or the lock renewal written at the same time. Writers of different kinds now never conflict. Success is the statement's num_affected_rows. The clauses are:

  • Upsert (runs, units): update when matched, insert otherwise.
  • Watermark compare-and-set: update when the stored cas_key equals the expected one (<=>), or equals the new one and was written by the same run (a replay); insert only when nothing is expected.
  • Lock: update when the stored lease has expired (expires_us <= now) or when the stored owner is the taker's own (t.owner = s.owner), insert when there is none. The owner is new for every acquisition, so the owner clause only matches a replay: a retry after a dropped Connect channel or Py4J connection whose first MERGE committed unseen finds its own row and succeeds, instead of raising LockHeld against itself. Zero affected rows means the lock is held: the row is read and LockHeld raised. Renewal is an UPDATE and release a DELETE, both filtered on the owner, run through the core lease helper. Times come from the client clock, as in the other stores.

A Delta concurrent-modification error is retried up to CONFLICT_RETRIES = 10 times with 50 to 500 ms of random jitter; the MERGE conditions are re-evaluated on the new snapshot, so a lost race turns into a clean false or LockHeld. Reads are filtered selects. The store reuses the Spark session it finds (the engine opens its session before the first state call, ADR-0030) and builds one from its session options only when none exists; it stops only a session it built.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Spark projects get shared state with no new service, on every Spark flavor the engine supports.
  • Each state call runs a Spark job (tens to hundreds of milliseconds); fine for a few calls per unit, slow for very wide runs.
  • The table grows with every run and unit; Delta's own OPTIMIZE and VACUUM apply. A retention command is a later concern.
  • Lease times rely on the clocks of the writers, as with the other stores.
  • The contract's cross-process lock test starts a second JVM, so it runs only with PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK_HEAVY=1. CI does not set it yet: on GitHub runners the child JVM stalled for over 240 s while resolving the Delta packages, before it reached the lock. Lock exclusion between writers is still covered in one process (the eight-thread race), and it rests on the same Delta commit check whether the writers share a JVM or not. Running the test in CI, for example with the Delta jars pre-resolved into a local directory, is a follow-up.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted. Amends ADR-0008.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: pipeloom 0.5 adds an orchestrator plugin that deploys a plan as a Databricks job. The core must stay free of any orchestrator, yet the plugin needs four things from it: a place for deploy options that the plan carries without changing its identity, a manifest that is byte-identical across compiles so a deployed copy can be compared, a way to add CLI commands, and secrets that resolve at run time without entering any recorded output. ADR-0004 (discovery), ADR-0010 (events and artifacts), ADR-0013 (run identity) and ADR-0014 (secrets by reference) each say something about these, and this ADR amends them. It covers the first half of the 0.5 core change; the finalize command, the orchestrator id and the link fallback for write_json_once follow in a second half.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• Deploy options as a model key or a new top-level section. Compute is a runtime setting a target may override, so a separate section would need its own precedence rules.
  • A deploy runtime key bound against the existing renderers plugin group. One precedence rule (target over top level), one options model per plugin, no new group of specs.
  • Resolve ${secret:...} at load time. Simple, but the value would reach the plan, the manifest and compile output.
  • Resolve it when the options of a plugin are bound for execution. The value lives in the plugin object only.
  • Commands through a new plugin spec group. A command is a click object, not a PluginSpec, so a spec would add nothing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
deploy is a runtime key (RuntimeSettings.deploy, a plugin block). Binding checks it against the renderers group: the kind must exist, and its options must validate against the spec's config_model, with line marks. The core never calls a renderer factory. The validated options, kind included, are recorded as PlanMetadata.deploy and written to the manifest under metadata.deploy, which is left out when the target has no deploy block. It is not in _HASHED_METADATA, so editing it leaves the plan hash unchanged. The JSON Schema shows deploy as a oneOf on kind, like the other plugin blocks.

manifest_bytes(plan, stable=True) blanks generated_at and invocation_id and empties the selection (select, exclude, selected), so one project and target always give the same bytes. write_manifest takes the same flag.

pipeloom.commands is a ninth entry-point group. Its entries name a click command and are discovered from metadata only: the module is imported when the command is invoked, never to list it, and --help lists plugin commands without importing them. A built-in command beats an entry point of the same name, and of several distributions providing one name the first by distribution name wins; both cases print a warning to stderr. A command that fails to import becomes a stub that prints the error and exits 1, so the rest of the CLI keeps working. PIPELOOM_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD hides every plugin command. plugins list --group commands lists them, and --check imports them. The group has no PluginSpec, so it is not part of GROUPS, only of the Group literal.

${secret:provider/path} references resolve only when a command executes, while the options of the plugins it builds are bound (run now; finalize with the second half). BoundPlugin.create(secrets) re-validates the options as written with each reference replaced, and the resolved value is registered with the redactor before any plugin that holds it is built. Providers come from the secret_providers group, are built once per invocation with default options, and a failure of any kind is PLX109 naming the provider and path, never a value. Compile, validate and the manifest only ever see the reference text. A resolved value is masked everywhere text leaves the process: the event bus, run_results.json (finalize), per-unit attempt files and state store rows (the runner), and the message of an internal error. Under boundary: task each unit process resolves and masks on its own. A plugin factory that fails while it holds resolved options is reported as PLX109 with a masked message and no chained traceback. The naming plugin is built at compile time and therefore never resolves secrets.

Only a reference written literally in the YAML resolves. The loader records the span of each one, also under secret-like keys, whose ${env:...} and ${var:...} are otherwise left alone. $${secret:provider/path} is the escape: it renders as the text ${secret:provider/path}, is never resolved and never asks for its provider, so an unknown provider is not an error there. Text that arrives through ${env:...} or ${var:...} and happens to look like a reference never resolves either. The built-in env provider reads the process environment, not the env mapping given to the API, so through the API ${secret:env/X} and ${env:X} can read different environments; the CLI passes the process environment to both.

The plugin API stays (0, 4). Every change is additive for plugins: a new runtime key, a new entry-point group read only by the CLI, and BoundPlugin.create gaining an optional argument that plugins never call.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: An orchestrator plugin can carry its options in the manifest without touching the plan hash, and can ship a manifest whose bytes do not depend on when it was compiled. A project with a deploy block fails with PLR204 where the renderer plugin is not installed, which is the point. Masking is by exact value: a plugin that transforms a secret (encodes or truncates it) before logging it defeats the redactor, and values shorter than four characters are never masked. A ${secret: reference in a place the core does not bind as plugin options (model SQL, vars) stays literal.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted.

docs.title: Incremental models
docs.text: An incremental model processes only the input rows that are new since its last run. pipeloom keeps a watermark, the largest value of one input column seen so far, and filters the input with it. The watermark is saved after the write succeeds, so a failed run never skips rows.

docs.title: A first incremental model
docs.text:
Project pipeloom.yml:

config_version: 1
name: shop
targets:
  dev:
    engine: {kind: polars}
    catalog: {kind: filesystem, root: target/warehouse}
    state: {kind: json, path: .pipeloom/state}

raw/orders.csv:

id,customer_id,amount,status,updated_at
1,10,5.0,paid,2026-01-01T10:00:00
2,10,2.5,new,2026-01-01T11:00:00
3,11,7.0,paid,2026-01-02T09:00:00

models/orders.yml:

sources:
  - name: raw_orders
    format: csv
    location: raw/orders.csv
    options: {try_parse_dates: true}   # read updated_at as a timestamp, not text
models:
  - name: orders
    sql: select id, customer_id, amount, status, updated_at from raw_orders
    inputs: {raw_orders: {source: raw_orders}}
    materialized: incremental
    incremental: {input: raw_orders, column: updated_at, lookback: 2h}
    write:
      strategy: merge
      unique_key: [id]

The incremental block names the input to filter (it must be one of the model's inputs), the column that moves forward, an optional lookback and where the watermark lives. Run it twice, adding rows to the CSV in between:

$ pipeloom run
... state.watermark_committed {'column': 'updated_at', 'dtype': 'timestamp[us]', 'before': None, 'after': '2026-01-02T09:00:00', ...}
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ incremental/merge   3 rows
$ printf '4,12,9.0,new,2026-01-03T09:00:00\n' >> raw/orders.csv
$ pipeloom run
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ incremental/merge   2 rows

The second run read only rows at or after 2026-01-02T07:00:00 (the watermark minus two hours), so it wrote 2 rows: the new order 4 and a re-merge of order 3 that falls inside the window.

docs.title: How a unit decides what to read
docs.text:
A unit runs incrementally when the materialization is incremental, the target table exists, the run is not a --full-refresh and a watermark is known. Otherwise it reads the whole input and writes the full result (the first build, or a rebuild).

  • Strict bound. With no lookback the filter is column > watermark. A row equal to the watermark is not read again.
  • Lookback. With lookback above zero the filter is column >= watermark - lookback. The value takes a duration (2h, 1d, or seconds). On a date column it is rounded up to whole days. Use it for data that arrives late. A lookback needs a timestamp or date column; on any other type the unit fails with PLM205.
  • Types. The column's type family (timestamp with a zone, timestamp without one, date, integer, decimal, float, string) must match the stored watermark, or the unit fails with PLM205. A column missing from the input is PLM205 too.
  • New watermark. After a successful write the watermark becomes the larger of the old one and the largest value in the batch. It never moves back, even when the lookback window returns older rows than the watermark.

A Python model sees the decision on its context:

def build(ctx, raw_orders):
    if ctx.is_incremental:
        ctx.log("incremental run", watermark=str(ctx.watermark), lower_bound=str(ctx.lower_bound))
    return raw_orders

ctx.is_incremental is true only on an incremental run. ctx.watermark and ctx.lower_bound are None otherwise. The input it receives is already filtered.

docs.title: Where the watermark lives
docs.text:
watermark_source has two values.

Value Behavior state (default) The watermark is stored in the state store under the project, target and model. If it is missing but the target table exists, pipeloom reads the maximum of the column from the target, uses it and records watermark_seeded: target in the unit's warnings. target The watermark is the maximum of the column in the target table, read on every run. The state store is never written.

Use target when the table itself is the truth, for example after restoring it from a backup, and you do not want a state store entry to disagree with it.

docs.title: Appending with a lookback
docs.text: With strategy: append and a lookback above zero, rows inside the window are written again on every run. pipeloom validate warns with PLP410. Use merge with a unique_key instead (see Merge, replace_partitions and schema changes). The default strategy of an incremental model that sets none is append.

docs.title: Full refresh and the first build
docs.text: pipeloom run --full-refresh ignores the watermark, reads the whole input and writes the table as an overwrite, whatever the strategy. The new watermark is the batch maximum. The first build (the target does not exist) also reads everything, and it keeps the declared strategy: into an absent table every strategy writes the same rows, and merge still checks its key.

docs.title: Retries, reruns and the watermark
docs.text:
The write stores the watermark it intends to commit, together with its idempotency token. If a run dies after the write and before the watermark is saved, rerunning with the same --run-id finds the token, skips the read, the body and the write, and commits that stored watermark. New rows that arrived in between are not skipped, because the retry never looked at them.

If the stored watermark changed while the unit ran, which usually means a second run on the same target, the unit fails with PLM203. The data is already written. Do not use --no-lock to run two runs of one target at once.

docs.title: What the run records
docs.text:
• Event state.watermark_committed with the column, type, before and after values, the source and whether the value was seeded.
  • In run_results.json: is_incremental, watermark_before and watermark_after, plus rows_inserted, rows_updated and rows_deleted for merge. See Run artifacts.
  • Engines that can run incremental models: polars and pandas (and the in-memory test engine).

docs.title: Data quality
docs.text: Expectations check a model's output before it is written. Each one has an action: warn, drop or fail. Dropped rows can go to a quarantine table so you can look at them later. The polars and pandas engines support all of it.

docs.title: Declare expectations
docs.text:
Project and source as in the quickstart, with this raw/orders.csv:

id,amount,status,updated_at
1,5.0,paid,2026-01-01T10:00:00
2,-2.5,paid,2026-01-01T11:00:00
3,7.0,refunded,2026-01-02T09:00:00
,4.0,new,2026-01-02T10:00:00

models/orders.yml:

sources:
  - name: raw_orders
    format: csv
    location: raw/orders.csv
    options: {try_parse_dates: true}
models:
  - name: orders
    sql: select id, amount, status, updated_at from raw_orders
    inputs: {raw_orders: {source: raw_orders}}
    expectations:
      - {name: id_present, check: {not_null: [id]}, on_violation: drop}
      - {name: status_known, check: {accepted_values: {column: status, values: [new, paid, shipped]}}, on_violation: drop}
      - {name: amount_non_negative, check: {range: {column: amount, min: 0}}, on_violation: warn}
      - {name: unique_id, check: {unique: [id]}, on_violation: fail}
      - {name: not_empty, check: {row_count: {min: 1}}, on_violation: fail}
    quality: {quarantine: true, max_drop_ratio: 0.5}

$ pipeloom run
... WARN   orders: id_present (not_null) dropped 1 of 4 rows
... WARN   orders: status_known (accepted_values) dropped 1 of 4 rows
... WARN   orders: amount_non_negative (range) failed on 1 of 4 rows
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ table/overwrite   2 rows

Two rows were written, two went to orders__quarantine, and the negative amount only produced a warning. The unit still succeeded. on_violation defaults to fail.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Row checks look at each row. check takes one of these (or use expr instead of check):

Check Passes when not_null: [a, b] the columns are not null accepted_values: {column, values} the value is one of the list (exact comparison) range: {column, min, max} the value is within the bounds, inclusive; either bound may be left out regex: {column, pattern} the pattern is found anywhere in the string (an unanchored search); the column must be a string expr: "amount >= 0" the expression is true

A null passes every check except not_null, and NaN counts as null. A row check can warn, drop or fail.

Aggregate checks look at the whole batch and can only warn or fail (a drop is PLP403):

Check Fails when unique: [a, b] a key appears more than once (rows with a null key part are not counted) row_count: {min, max} the number of rows is outside the bounds freshness: {column, max_age} the newest value is older than max_age; an all-null column fails

Aggregates see the rows that are left after drops. For an incremental model that means the new rows of this run, not the whole table.

docs.title: The expr dialect
docs.text: An expr is written in the dialect of the engine and never runs code. On polars it is a SQL expression (amount >= 0 and amount < 1e6). On pandas it is a restricted Python expression: column names, literals, comparisons, and, or, not, arithmetic and in with a list. Function calls, attributes and @name are rejected with PLQ302. Prefer the named checks when a model has to run on several engines.

docs.title: Drops, quarantine and the drop ratio
docs.text:
A row that fails any drop check is removed from the output. With quality.quarantine: true the removed rows are appended to <target>__quarantine: the model's columns plus

Column Content _pipeloom_run_id the run that dropped the row _pipeloom_failed the names of the failed drop checks (a list; JSON text on a csv catalog) _pipeloom_ts when it happened, a UTC timestamp

quality.max_drop_ratio (0 to 1) fails the unit when the share of dropped rows is larger. In the example, 0.25 fails the unit because half of the rows are dropped:

FAIL   orders ... PLQ301
  model 'orders' failed expectation(s): max_drop_ratio
  hint: fix the data, or relax on_violation or quality.max_drop_ratio

A failed fail check or an exceeded ratio stops the unit before it writes: the target and its quarantine are left as they were. The counts are still recorded. Quarantine rows are written once per run even if the unit is retried. If the model output changes, the quarantine table follows (new columns are added); an incompatible type change fails with PLM202 naming the quarantine table.

A view or an ephemeral model cannot carry expectations (PLP411), and no other model may be called <model>__quarantine in the same schema (PLP412). An engine that does not declare the quality capability is rejected with PLC510.

docs.title: What the run records
docs.text:
• model.quality_evaluated event: total rows, one result per expectation, dropped and quarantined counts, the drop ratio and the names of the failures.
  • run_results.json: expectations[] (name, kind, action, passed, failed and, for aggregates, a value), rows_dropped, rows_quarantined and warnings[]. See Run artifacts.
  • The console prints a WARN line for every check that warned, dropped or failed rows.

Counts are kept for fail checks too, so you can see how bad a failing batch was.

docs.title: Retries, timeouts and cancellation
docs.text: A unit can fail for a reason that goes away on its own, run for too long, or be stopped together with the run. pipeloom has a setting for each case.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
sources:
  - {name: raw_orders, format: csv, location: raw/orders.csv}
models:
  - name: orders
    python: shop.flaky:load
    inputs: {raw_orders: {source: raw_orders}}
    retries: 2          # extra attempts after the first; the default is 0
    retry_delay: 1s     # base delay; the default is 1s
    retry_on: transient # or "any"
    timeout: 5m

The model above fails once with a TransientError and then succeeds:

$ pipeloom run
... 1/1 FAIL   orders ........ PLX101 pipeloom.engine.errors.TransientError
... RETRY  orders attempt 1 failed PLX101 (transient), next in 0.7s
... 1/1 OK     orders ........ table/overwrite   2 rows

Each attempt writes its own file (units/orders/attempt-1.json, attempt-2.json), and the result row has attempt: 2 and retries_used: 1. While a unit waits for its next attempt it holds no worker slot, and every attempt emits unit.retrying with the attempt that failed, the next one and the delay.

retries, retry_delay, retry_on and timeout can be set in defaults and in a model.

docs.title: What is retried
docs.text:
With retry_on: transient (the default) only transient failures are retried. A failure is transient when:

  • the model or an engine raised pipeloom.engine.errors.TransientError, directly or as the cause of another exception;
  • the engine says so (for example a table commit conflict);
  • a ConnectionError or TimeoutError is in the cause chain;
  • an OSError happened while reading, writing or touching state, except file not found, permission denied and the directory errors (a Windows sharing violation counts as transient);
  • a unit process exited without a result (PLX106).

Everything else is permanent: an exception from your code, a validation error and a failed expectation. A rejected schema change, a lost watermark race, a bad watermark and a bad write key are always permanent. With retry_on: any every failed attempt is retried, including deterministic ones, so use it only when you know that a rerun can change the outcome.

An append model on an engine without idempotent writes cannot have retries (PLC505), because a retry could write the same rows twice. The polars and pandas engines have idempotent writes.

docs.title: Delay between attempts
docs.text: For retry number n the delay is a random value between half and all of min(max(retry_delay, 300 s), retry_delay * 2^(n-1)). With the default of one second that is up to 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on, capped at five minutes. The random part is seeded by the run id, the unit and n, so the same run waits the same time.

docs.title: Who retries
docs.text: Whoever schedules the unit. With boundary: process or task under pipeloom run, the parent scheduler retries. A single unit run with --select unit:<id>, which is what an orchestrator task does, never retries on its own: the orchestrator owns the retry.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
timeout is a limit per attempt. A unit that exceeds it ends as timed_out with PLX102, its downstream units are skipped and the run fails. A timeout is never retried.

... 2/2 TIMEOUT slow_orders ... PLX102 after 2s (attempt 1)

pipeloom cannot kill a Python thread. On the thread executor (boundary: process) the attempt is asked to stop and then abandoned: the unit is marked timed_out at once and whatever the thread reports later is dropped. The engine's cancel is called once. The model stops at the checkpoints before reading, after the body and before the write; a long call in the middle of your code is not interrupted. If the thread is still working when the run ends, run.completed reports it in abandoned_threads, and the thread ends with the process. In the rare case where an abandoned thread still commits its write, the attempt file says timed_out and the unit gets a late_result: <status> warning. With boundary: task the child process is killed after timeout plus the grace period, together with everything it started.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C (or send SIGTERM; on Windows, Ctrl+C or Ctrl+Break) to stop a run:

  1. The first signal is a graceful stop. Nothing new starts, pending, queued and retrying units are cancelled, and running units are asked to stop. They get cancel_grace seconds to finish, and a unit that finishes in time keeps its real result. The rest end as cancelled (PLX104). The run emits run.cancel_requested, ends with status cancelled and exits with 130.
  2. A second signal is a hard stop: no more grace; running units are cancelled at once.
  3. A third signal raises KeyboardInterrupt.

cancel_grace is 30 seconds by default. Set it per target, or override it for one run:

targets:
  dev:
    engine: {kind: polars}
    catalog: {kind: filesystem, root: target/warehouse}
    state: {kind: json, path: .pipeloom/state}
    cancel_grace: 10s

$ pipeloom run --cancel-grace 5s

From Python, pass a RunControl to Project.run(..., control=control) and call control.request_stop().

With boundary: task each child runs in its own process group, so a Ctrl+C in your terminal reaches only the parent, which then stops the children. A graceful stop is SIGTERM on POSIX and Ctrl+Break on Windows, followed by a kill after the grace. Windows has no job objects in 0.3: a grandchild started by a child that exits on its own can outlive the run.

Run IDs are reusable after a stop. Rerun with the same --run-id and the units that already committed are skipped through their write tokens.

docs.title: Running a pipeline
docs.text:
pipeloom run executes the selected models of a project and writes the run artifacts.

$ pipeloom run --target polars

The command validates the project, compiles the plan, takes a run lock, runs every selected unit in dependency order and finalizes the artifacts. Exit codes: 0 when every unit succeeded, 1 when a unit or a check failed, 2 for bad usage and 130 when the run was stopped.

Select models with -s/--select and --exclude (see pipeloom ls). A unit whose upstream failed is skipped with the reason upstream_failed. With --fail-fast the first failure stops the scheduler from starting more units; the units still waiting are skipped with the reason fail_fast. Independent branches keep running without it.

docs.title: Executors and the boundary
docs.text:
The target's boundary decides how units are executed. You can override it with --boundary.

Boundary Executor What it does process (default) thread Every unit runs on a thread of the invocation. One engine session serves all of them, and an ephemeral model shared by several units is computed once. task process Every unit runs as its own pipeloom run --select unit:<id> process, so each unit could be an orchestrator task. Events of the child are relayed to the parent, and its logs go to logs/.

--workers N (or PIPELOOM_WORKERS) sets how many units run at once. The default is the target's workers setting, else the smaller of 4 and the CPU count.

With boundary: task the units share nothing in memory, so the state store must be shared between processes: the json store qualifies, sqlite does not (PLC503). Starting a child process costs about a second per unit.

docs.title: Run ids and reruns
docs.text:
Each run has an id: --run-id, or a timestamp and a short suffix such as 20261104T014938Z-3fa91c. Ids use 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens.

Reusing a run id continues that run. Every write carries the idempotency token <run_id>:<unit_id>, and the filesystem catalog remembers the last tokens of each table, so a unit that already committed under that token is not written twice. Rerunning a finished run with the same id leaves the data byte-identical. Attempt files keep counting up (attempt-2.json, and so on), and run_results.json reports the newest attempt of each unit.

Every engine sees one start time for the run. By default it is the time the run began, and a reused run id keeps the start recorded the first time. --run-started-at ISO8601 (or PIPELOOM_RUN_STARTED_AT) sets it instead, for an orchestrator that wants every task to share the job's start time. The value needs a UTC offset (2026-11-05T03:00:00+00:00 or a trailing Z) and needs --run-id. Giving a different value for a run id that already has a start is PLX108 and exit code 2. The Spark engine derives its Delta write version from this time.

--full-refresh rebuilds append tables from scratch. It takes an optional true or false, so an orchestrator can pass a templated value.

To run exactly the plan you compiled earlier, pass --manifest target/runs/<id>/manifest.json. Add --expect-plan-hash <sha256> to stop with PLX103 when the plan changed.

docs.title: Intermediates
docs.text:
A model with materialized: intermediate is persisted for the length of the run, so units in other processes (boundary: task) can read it. The result goes to <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model> and relation_name in run_results.json is that location. An intermediate takes no incremental block, no partition_by and no strategy other than overwrite (PLP413).

The target setting artifacts: {intermediate_ttl: 1d} (default 1d) says how long the data stays. With 0 the folder is deleted at the end of a run that succeeded; a failed run keeps it. At the end of every run, finalize also deletes the intermediates of other runs once they are older than the TTL those runs recorded. A run that left no results, or was resumed and stopped again, is deleted after it has been idle for the longer of the TTL and one hour. A deletion that fails is a warning in run.warnings, never a failed run.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text: A run takes a lock named <project>/<target> in the state store, so two runs of one target do not overlap. The lock is a lease of 60 seconds that a heartbeat renews every 20 seconds. A run that dies frees the lock within a minute. A second run that finds the lock held stops with PLX105 and names the holder, its run id and when the lease expires. --no-lock skips the lock.

docs.title: Unit mode for orchestrators
docs.text: pipeloom run --select unit:<id> runs a single execution unit and nothing else: no lock, no run.* events, no run_results.json. Use it when an orchestrator owns the schedule and the retries. Each invocation writes its own attempt file and event file under the run folder, and the invocation that owns the run merges them when it finalizes. The unit ids are in the manifest.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: The console prints one line per unit, a summary, the failure block for each failed unit and the paths of the files written. See Run artifacts for the files.

docs.title: Merge, replace_partitions and schema changes
docs.text: write.strategy decides how a batch meets the rows already in the target table. 0.3 adds merge and replace_partitions next to append and overwrite, and a policy for batches whose columns differ from the table. The polars and pandas engines support all of it on filesystem tables.

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
Rows are matched on unique_key. Matched rows are updated, unmatched rows are inserted.

models:
  - name: orders
    python: shop.orders:build
    inputs: {raw_orders: {source: raw_orders}}
    materialized: incremental
    incremental: {input: raw_orders, column: updated_at, lookback: 2h}
    write:
      strategy: merge
      unique_key: [id]
      update_condition: "source.updated_at > target.updated_at"
      deletes: {column: status, value: cancelled, mode: hard}
  • update_condition is optional and written in the engine's dialect (a SQL expression on polars, a restricted Python expression on pandas). source.x is the batch, target.x the table, and a bare name means the source. A matched row whose condition is false or null is left unchanged.
  • deletes marks batch rows as deletions: a row where column equals value removes the matched target row with mode: hard, or writes the batch row with mode: soft so you can keep a flag. A delete for a key that is not in the table is ignored. The update_condition applies to deletes too.
  • A batch with a repeated key, or without the key column, fails with PLM206 before anything is written. A row with a null key never matches and is inserted.
  • run_results.json reports rows_inserted, rows_updated and rows_deleted; rows_written counts inserts, updates and soft deletes.

In 0.3 a merge reads the whole table, merges in memory and rewrites it, so its cost grows with the table. Row order is not preserved.

docs.title: replace_partitions
docs.text:
replace_partitions swaps the partitions present in the batch and leaves the others alone. It needs partition_by; without it pipeloom validate reports PLP407.

models:
  - name: daily_clicks
    sql: select event_date, user_id, clicks from raw_events
    inputs: {raw_events: {source: raw_events}}
    partition_by: [event_date]
    write:
      strategy: replace_partitions
      on_schema_change: append_new_columns

With partition_by every strategy writes one part file per distinct partition value. A replace_partitions write drops the files of the partitions in the batch and adds the new ones without reading the other files. rows_deleted reports how many old rows went away. A table written by 0.2 has no partition values in its files, so the first replace reads and rewrites those files once. An empty batch changes no files. A null is a partition value like any other.

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text:
write.on_schema_change says what happens when the batch's columns differ from the target's. The default is fail.

Policy Result fail Any added, removed or retyped column is PLM202. ignore The table keeps its columns. Extra batch columns are dropped, missing ones are filled with nulls, values are cast to the table's types (a failed cast is PLM201). append_new_columns The table's columns plus the new ones, which are nullable. Removed columns stay. A type change is PLM202. sync_all_columns The batch's columns. A type change is accepted only if it widens.

Widening means a wider integer, an integer to float64, float32 to float64, a decimal that keeps every digit, a finer timestamp unit in the same zone, or a null column to any type. A batch that differs from the table only by such a widening of the table's type is cast to the table's type under every policy.

The policy applies to append, merge and replace_partitions on an existing table. overwrite, --full-refresh and the first build use the batch's schema, and report the difference with the action replaced.

With fail, adding a column to the model fails like this:

FAIL   daily_clicks ... PLM202
  schema change rejected for model 'daily_clicks' (on_schema_change: fail): the batch schema
  differs from the target: added extra (int32)
  hint: change the model, or set write.on_schema_change to ignore, append_new_columns or sync_all_columns

With append_new_columns the same run succeeds and prints one line:

daily_clicks: schema changed on main.daily_clicks (policy append_new_columns, applied): +device string

Each change is an event model.schema_changed (relation, policy, action and the list of changes), and schema_changes[] of the unit in run_results.json carries the same diff. The filesystem catalog reads every old file through the table's current schema, so adding a column or widening a type never rewrites existing files. A key column (unique_key or partition_by) missing from the batch is PLM206, whatever the policy.

docs.title: Safe concurrent writes
docs.text: A filesystem table commit takes a lock file with a 30 second lease and checks that nobody committed since the table was read. If another writer got in first, the second fails with a transient error and can be rerun from the new version. Do not run two writers on one table on purpose; the run lock exists to prevent it.

docs.title: pandas engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-pandas runs models on pandas DataFrames.

$ pip install "pipeloom[pandas]"

targets:
  dev:
    engine: {kind: pandas}
    catalog: {kind: filesystem, root: warehouse}
    state: {kind: json, path: .pipeloom/state}

The engine needs the filesystem catalog: tables are directories of part files committed through _pipeloom/commit.json (ADR-0022). Any other catalog is rejected when the session opens.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, ephemeral Expectations and quarantine yes (expr limited to column names, literals and operators) SQL models and views no Idempotent writes yes, by run token Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes Cancel no

A SQL model on this engine is rejected with PLC502 and a view with PLC507. An intermediate materialization is supported (files under the artifacts root). incremental is supported. SQL on pandas is deferred past 0.2. The supported versions are pandas>=2.3.3,<4 and pyarrow>=22.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Relations are eager DataFrames, so rows_read is filled in run_results.json. A Python model receives DataFrame inputs and returns a DataFrame. With frame_api: narwhals the model receives Narwhals frames and returns a Narwhals or a native frame. Inputs are shared between the units that read them, so a model must not modify an input in place.

Reads use Arrow-backed columns (dtype_backend="pyarrow"): integer columns with nulls stay integers and the logical types of a table survive a round trip. String columns, object dtype in pandas 2 or the string dtype in pandas 3, are reported as string.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text: A table is written as one part file in the catalog format (parquet, csv or ndjson). Repeating a run id with the same token returns the stored result and writes nothing. A failure leaves the previous commit untouched and removes the unfinished part file. Reading a table concatenates its committed part files; csv and ndjson parts are cast back to the logical types stored in the commit file.

docs.title: Polars engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-polars runs models on Polars lazy frames.

$ pip install "pipeloom[polars]"

targets:
  dev:
    engine: {kind: polars}
    catalog: {kind: filesystem, root: warehouse}
    state: {kind: json, path: .pipeloom/state}

The engine needs the filesystem catalog: tables are directories of part files committed through _pipeloom/commit.json (ADR-0022). Any other catalog is rejected when the session opens.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, view, ephemeral Expectations and quarantine yes (expr through pl.sql_expr) SQL models and views yes, through pl.SQLContext Idempotent writes yes, by run token Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes Cancel no

incremental and intermediate are supported; an intermediate is a table of part files under the artifacts root. The polars bound is polars>=1.30,<3.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Relations are LazyFrames, so rows_read is empty in run_results.json. A Python model receives LazyFrame inputs and returns a LazyFrame or a DataFrame. With frame_api: narwhals the model receives Narwhals frames and returns a Narwhals or a native frame.

import narwhals.stable.v2 as nw


def fct_orders(ctx, enriched):
    return enriched.filter(nw.col("amount") > 1)

docs.title: SQL and views
docs.text: Each SQL model runs in a fresh pl.SQLContext that holds only its declared inputs, so aliases do not leak between models. A view stores its SQL and inputs in the commit file and is evaluated again on every read, so it sees later overwrites of its inputs. Rerunning with an unchanged definition commits nothing.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text: A table is collected and written as one part file in the catalog format (parquet, csv or ndjson). Repeating a run id with the same token returns the stored result and writes nothing. A failure leaves the previous commit untouched and removes the unfinished part file. A whole table must fit in memory in 0.2.

docs.title: Reading CSV and NDJSON tables
docs.text: Part files in csv and ndjson lose some type information, so a table is read back with the logical types stored in the commit file when this engine can name them all.

docs.title: Spark engine
docs.text:
pipeloom-spark runs models on Apache Spark DataFrames and Spark SQL and writes Delta Lake tables. It works on a local Spark, through Spark Connect, and inside a session someone else owns, such as a Databricks runtime. It also provides the table state store, which keeps run state in a Delta table.

$ pip install "pipeloom[spark]"      # local Spark: pulls pipeloom-spark[local]
$ pip install pipeloom-spark         # Databricks, Databricks Connect, or any environment with pyspark

targets:
  dev:
    engine: {kind: spark, mode: local, conf: {spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "4"}}
    catalog: {kind: delta_path, root: warehouse}
    state: {kind: table, path: warehouse/_state}

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pyspark is not a hard dependency. Databricks runtimes and Databricks Connect ship their own pyspark, and installing another one breaks them, so pipeloom-spark depends only on pipeloom.

Where Install Local Spark (a laptop, CI) pipeloom-spark[local], or pipeloom[spark]. The extra installs pyspark[connect] (4.0.1 up to, not including, 4.3) and delta-spark (4.1 up to, not including, 4.5). A Databricks runtime or serverless pipeloom-spark with no extras. Databricks Connect pipeloom-spark with no extras, next to databricks-connect. A thin Spark Connect client pipeloom-spark and pyspark-client. Never together with pyspark: both own the pyspark package.

Local Spark needs Java 17 or 21 on the path. Spark 4 runs with ANSI mode on by default, so an invalid cast or an overflow fails the query instead of giving null. Check SQL models that relied on the old behavior.

On Windows, run Spark in WSL. Windows Python workers do not work without winutils and die with a connection reset. Install Java and uv in the WSL distribution and run the project there.

docs.title: Session modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior local Builds a session with master (default local[*]), app_name and conf, and adds the Delta jars, SQL extension and catalog unless delta: false. connect Builds a Spark Connect session from remote or SPARK_REMOTE. A URL that starts with local starts a local Connect server with the same conf. active Uses the existing session and never builds, configures or stops anything. auto (default) active when DATABRICKS_RUNTIME_VERSION is set or a session exists, else connect when remote or SPARK_REMOTE is set, else local.

Only a session the engine built is stopped. The engine sets no Spark conf on a session it did not build, and sets none at run time on any session: conf applies when the session is built, and conf with mode active is an error. Building a session when one already exists in the process fails and tells you to use mode active. Classic and Connect cannot share one Python process.

boundary: task with local Spark starts one JVM per unit. It works, and it is slow.

docs.title: Catalogs
docs.text:
• delta_path: Delta tables at <root>/<schema>/<name>; the target's catalog name is ignored. No metastore, and it works across processes. root may be a URI such as s3:// or abfss://. It cannot hold views.
  • spark_catalog: tables and views by name through the session catalog (catalog option, else the current catalog). It is the base the Unity Catalog support of a later release reuses. A view is created with CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW over a table, delta or parquet input.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Capability Value Source formats delta, parquet, csv, json, ndjson Write strategies append, overwrite, merge, replace_partitions Materializations table, incremental, view, ephemeral, intermediate Expectations and quarantine yes SQL models and views yes, inputs bound by alias; views on spark_catalog Idempotent writes yes, by token in the Delta commit Metrics rows and bytes, from the commit history Cancel yes, through Spark job tags Portable frames (frame_api: narwhals) yes

csv reads a header and infers types; json is one multi-line document and ndjson is one document per line. Reader options pass through as strings.

docs.title: Write strategies
docs.text:
Every write is a DataFrameWriter option or a SQL statement. No Spark conf is touched.

Strategy What the engine does append Appends. New columns are added in the same write (mergeSchema). overwrite Overwrites data and schema (overwriteSchema), so any result of the schema policy is accepted. replace_partitions Overwrites with a replaceWhere predicate built from the distinct partition_by tuples of the batch. It works on partitioned and unpartitioned tables. More than 10,000 distinct tuples fails and recommends merge. An empty batch replaces nothing and writes only the token commit. merge A SQL MERGE INTO on unique_key, with update_condition and hard or soft deletes. Rows with a null key never match and are inserted. A key repeated in the batch is PLM206. A merge into a table that does not exist yet is the first load, written as an append.

A full refresh and a first build follow the core rules described in the write strategies guide.

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text: The core decides the final columns from on_schema_change. The engine writes added columns in the write itself (mergeSchema); a merge first makes an empty mergeSchema append instead. When columns were removed or a type was widened, the engine first runs one migration commit: it reads the table, aligns it to the final columns and overwrites it with overwriteSchema, keeping the table's partitioning. The migration commit carries no transaction options and no token, so it is not counted in the metrics. With the guard on, the claim commit made just before it takes the write version (see below).

docs.title: Tables created by spark_catalog
docs.text: A table that saveAsTable creates does not keep the writer's commit metadata. When the target does not exist, the catalog creates it empty first, without a token, and the tokened write is an ordinary append into it.

docs.title: Idempotent writes
docs.text:
Each write has the token <run_id>:<model>, which the engine records in Delta.

  • The transaction app id is pipeloom/<project>/<model>. Quarantine and intermediate writes add the suffix #quarantine or #intermediate.
  • The transaction version is the run start in epoch milliseconds. It comes from the run start time the core passes with the write (see --run-started-at in Running a pipeline), never from the session.
  • The commit's userMetadata holds {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "token", "commit_meta", "result"}}.

Before a write, the engine scans the last 100 commits (DESCRIBE HISTORY) for the token. A hit returns the stored result and writes nothing, so rerunning a finished run id changes no data.

For a merge, Delta applies the transaction options to a MERGE only through session conf, which would leak into other units of the same session. So the MERGE runs as plain SQL, and with the guard on it is bracketed by two empty appends:

  1. A claim commit before it, with the real transaction app id and version and the metadata {"pipeloom": {"v": 1, "claim": token}}. It has no token, so the token scan and the metrics ignore it. Delta refuses it when a later version exists, so PLM207 comes before any data changes. Any write that needs a migration commit makes the same claim first.
  2. A token commit after it, with the token and the stored result. The commits after the claim use the app id <app id>@<token> with version 1, which still keeps two attempts of the same token from both committing.

Running the same MERGE again with the same batch converges on the same table, so a crash between the commits is safe: the retry finds its own claim and continues. A claim is void once a later run of the same model has committed, so such a retry fails with PLM207 instead of merging over that run's data.

docs.title: PLM207 and its limits
docs.text:
The transaction version only grows. When Delta skips a write and no commit carries the token, the engine looks again (a racing attempt may have won), then through the full history. If the token is nowhere, a later version already exists for this model and the write fails with PLM207. Nothing was written, for every strategy: the claim commit makes the check come before any data or schema change. The causes:

  • a newer run of the same model finished first;
  • an overlapping run started with --no-lock;
  • a host clock that is behind, since the version comes from a timestamp. Clock skew between machines that write the same model can refuse a legitimate write.

PLM207 is permanent: retry_on: transient does not repeat it. To turn the guard off, set txn_guard: false on the engine. Then no transaction options are sent and only the history check applies, which still stops a repeated token, but nothing stops an older run from writing after a newer one.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Rows and bytes come from the table's commit history, so there is no extra Spark job. Before the write the engine notes the latest version. After it, the engine sums operationMetrics over the commits after that version whose token is this write's, plus the newest MERGE commit for a merge. Fields a commit does not report stay null in run_results.json.

A concurrent MERGE on the same table inside that window can be mistaken for ours in the metrics (the data is not affected).

docs.title: Expectations and quarantine
docs.text: The engine declares the quality capability. All counts and aggregates of a model's checks are evaluated in one Spark job. Rows dropped by a check go to <model>__quarantine with the usual _pipeloom_run_id, _pipeloom_failed and _pipeloom_ts columns, under the #quarantine app id. regex is a Java regular expression applied unanchored.

docs.title: The table state store
docs.text:
state: {kind: table, table: ops._pipeloom_state}   # by catalog name
# state: {kind: table, path: warehouse/_state}     # or by path; set exactly one of the two

table keeps watermarks, runs, units and the run lock in one Delta table, partitioned by kind. It is shared, so it works with boundary: task (PLC503 passes). Compare-and-set and the lock lease are single MERGE statements, and Delta conflicts are retried up to 10 times. The store reuses the engine's session; its session option builds one only when none exists, and only a session it built is stopped. Each state call is a Spark job, so it is slower than sqlite or json. The table grows with every run, and Delta's OPTIMIZE and VACUUM apply to it. Lease times use the client clock.

docs.title: Intermediates
docs.text: materialized: intermediate writes the model's result as a Delta table under <artifacts.root>/runs/<run_id>/intermediate/<model>, under the #intermediate app id. The consumer reads it back as a Delta path. With a remote Spark Connect server, the client and the server must both see artifacts.root, so set it to a shared location such as a Volume or an object-store URI. See Running a pipeline for the TTL.

docs.title: SQL
docs.text: A SQL model's inputs are bound without session temp views: each alias becomes a common table expression over a DataFrame passed to spark.sql, so two units can use the same alias at the same time and an alias shadows a catalog table of the same name.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Each unit adds a job tag (pipeloom:<run id>:<unit id>) for the length of its reads, body, checks and write. cancel interrupts the jobs with that tag (SparkContext job tags on classic Spark, session tags on Connect) and keeps interrupting, for up to a minute, until the unit ends. Cancellation is cooperative: Python code between jobs is not stopped, and a Delta commit either completes or does not happen.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text: The engine reads timestamps as microseconds since the epoch, so the Python process time zone never changes a value. User code that calls collect() on a classic session gets naive local datetimes for timestamp columns, converted in the time zone of the Python process. Convert in Spark (for example with unix_micros) when the exact instant matters.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text: Spark tests opt in with PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK=classic or connect and skip otherwise (pyspark, java on the path and a non-Windows host are needed). Classic and Connect run as two pytest invocations. A test that starts a second JVM also needs PIPELOOM_TEST_SPARK_HEAVY=1.

docs.title: Run artifacts
docs.text: A run writes its files under the artifacts root, target by default (set it with artifacts.root on the target). Paths in artifacts are POSIX.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
target/
  manifest.json            copy of the latest run's manifest
  run_results.json         copy of the latest run's results
  runs/<run_id>/
    manifest.json          the plan that ran (pipeloom.manifest/1)
    run_results.json       the outcome of the run (pipeloom.run_results/1)
    events/<invocation_id>.jsonl   events of each invocation
    units/<unit_id>/attempt-<n>.json   one file per attempt of a unit
    logs/<unit_id>-attempt-<n>.log     output of a task-boundary unit
    intermediate/<model>/          result of an `intermediate` model, deleted after `artifacts.intermediate_ttl`

Finalize writes run_results.json into the run folder, then copies it and the manifest to the root. The run folder is the source of truth; the root copies are for convenience.

Finalize also deletes the intermediate/ folder of other runs once they are idle. A finished run is judged by the intermediate_ttl it recorded. A run with no run_results.json, or whose manifest is newer than its results (resumed, then possibly crashed again), is judged by the newest modification time under its run folder and expires after max(ttl, 1h) of inactivity, so an active run is never deleted.

docs.title: Attempt files
docs.text: Each unit writes units/<unit_id>/attempt-<n>.json when the attempt ends, whatever the outcome. The file holds one results row, the same object that appears in run_results.json. The runner writes it, so it exists for a unit that ran in a child process too. A reused run id keeps counting: the next attempt is one above the highest file. A unit that started under boundary: task and left no attempt file is reported as failed with PLX106, with the end of its log as the excerpt.

docs.title: run_results.json
docs.text:
schema is pipeloom.run_results/1. Top-level keys:

Key Content schema The schema name and version. metadata pipeloom_version, generated_at, invocation_id, plugins. args The options of the invocation: select, exclude, manifest, run_id, full_refresh, fail_fast, workers, boundary, lock. run One object for the whole run, below. results One row per persisted model, sorted by unit_id.

run holds run_id, parent_run_id (null in 0.2), invocation_ids (every invocation that worked on the run), project, target, plan_hash, selector, full_refresh, status (succeeded, failed or cancelled), started_at, ended_at, duration_ms, counts (total and one number per unit status), totals (rows_written and bytes_written of succeeded units), identity (user, host, orchestrator, orchestrator_ids), pipeloom_version, plugins, python_version, git_sha (null outside a git repository), exit_code, intermediate_ttl (seconds; the TTL this run was finalized with, which other runs use to judge its intermediates) and warnings (run-level messages, such as intermediate_cleanup_failed: <run_id>: <error> when an expired folder could not be deleted).

Every row in results has every key. Ephemeral models have no row: they appear in the ephemeral_inlined list of the units that inline them.

Field Meaning unique_id, unit_id Model id (model.<project>.<name>) and execution unit id. ephemeral_inlined Ephemeral models computed inside this unit. materialization, strategy, relation_name What was built and where. status succeeded, failed, skipped or cancelled. skip_reason upstream_failed or fail_fast for a skipped unit, else null. attempt, retries_used Attempt number; retries are 0 in 0.2. started_at, ended_at, duration_ms, queue_wait_ms Timing. Timestamps are RFC 3339 UTC. rows_read Rows read per input alias; null where the engine is lazy (polars). rows_written, rows_inserted, bytes_written Write metrics; null when the engine does not report them. full_refresh, is_incremental Whether the unit was rebuilt from scratch; incremental is false in 0.2. schema_hash sha256 of the canonical output schema (name, dtype, nullable, in column order). error Null, or code, category (transient or permanent), message, hint, exception_type, trace_excerpt. engine, engine_version, executor What ran the unit (thread or process). idempotency_token <run_id>:<unit_id>.

Incremental and merge models fill rows_updated, rows_deleted, target_version, is_incremental, watermark_before and watermark_after (ISO text for dates and timestamps), and warnings carries watermark_seeded: target when the state store had no watermark. Fields that later versions fill stay null or empty: rows_dropped, rows_quarantined, bytes_read, schema_changes, expectations and orchestrator_ids.

There is no published JSON Schema for this file yet. It is described here and covered by golden tests; a schema under schema/v1/ will follow once the field set stops moving.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: events/<invocation_id>.jsonl holds the events of one invocation, one JSON object per line. An invocation that runs a single unit writes only its own file; the owning invocation forwards the unit events it receives, keeping the original invocation id and sequence number. Order events across files by (ts, invocation_id, seq).

docs.title: pipeloom run
docs.text:
Run the selected models. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 a unit or a check failed, 2 bad usage, 130 stopped.

The first Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops starting units and gives running ones --cancel-grace to finish; a second one kills them at once; a third raises KeyboardInterrupt.

-s unit:NAME runs one unit without a lock or run results, and never retries it; the process executor uses it.

Usage:

pipeloom run [OPTIONS]

Options:

  --project-dir DIRECTORY    Directory that holds pipeloom.yml.  [default: .]
  --vars TEXT                Variables as a YAML or JSON mapping; they
                             override the vars block.
  --target TEXT              Target to bind; default_target or the only target
                             when omitted.
  --plugin MODULE:ATTR       A PluginSpec to load besides the installed
                             plugins. Repeatable.
  -s, --select SELECTOR      Models to include: name, tag:x, path:dir,
                             materialized:x, +model, model+, N+model, model+N.
                             Space unions, comma intersects. Repeatable, all
                             are unioned.
  --exclude SELECTOR         Remove the models this selector matches from the
                             selection. Repeatable.
  --log-format [text|json]   Diagnostics and events on stderr: readable text
                             or one JSON object per line.  [default: text]
  --manifest FILE            Run the plan of this manifest instead of
                             compiling the project.
  --expect-plan-hash HEX     Stop with PLX103 unless the plan hash is this
                             sha256.
  --run-id TEXT              Name of the run. Reusing it continues that run.
                             Default: a timestamp and a suffix.
  --full-refresh BOOLEAN     Rebuild append tables from scratch. Takes an
                             optional true or false.  [default: False]
  --run-started-at ISO8601   Start time of the run, with a UTC offset (for
                             example the start of the orchestrator job).
                             Engines use it to make writes idempotent. Needs
                             --run-id. A reused run id keeps the start it
                             recorded.
  --fail-fast                After the first failure, start no more units.
  --no-lock                  Do not take the run lock.
  --workers INTEGER RANGE    Units to run at once. Default: the target's
                             setting, else min(4, CPUs).  [x>=1]
  --boundary [process|task]  process runs units on threads here; task runs
                             each in its own process. Default: the target's
                             boundary.
  --warn-error               Exit 1 on warnings too.
  --cancel-grace DURATION    After a stop request (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM) or a
                             timeout, how long running units may finish before
                             they are killed, as 30s, 2m or 30. Default: the
                             setting, else 30s.
  --help                     Show this message and exit.
